lens: World model and affordances: entities, items, ownership, construction and destruction, and how options are enumerated for JEV
summary: Fernhollow has no world model that villagers can change. The world is a hand-laid, fixed tile grid (town-map.ts:3 says "Hand-laid and fixed"), 21 fixed buildings with no owner, durability or contents, and a set of one-off containers: one footbridge project, one chapel pantry, a homeFood map, and three shops keyed by a closed "store"|"diner"|"inn" union. Items are a single undifferentiated "food" number plus coins. Building uses no materials, and nothing can be damaged, repaired, moved or claimed. The engine writes to tiles in only two places (a grave, the bridge), the renderer assumes graves are the only tiles that change, and homeOf() throws when someone has no home, so destroying a house would crash the sim. Ownership only exists implicitly and case by case, and so does grievance: 23 nudgeAffinity calls with hand-tuned constants and a closed CrimeKind list. "Destroy someone's house and they are pissed" cannot even be expressed. On the affordance side, buildOptions is 484 hand-written lines, and each verb touches about 9 code sites. Menus run a median of 30 options (max 52), with 13 options that appear in essentially every menu. Kindness verbs only ever target the single nearest person. I measured that when a household member is in sight, none of them can be given to, lent to or complimented in 62-81% of decisions. The fix: a generic Thing table (location, owner, hp, contents, version), item bundles with recipes, a verb table with one executor, a generic Harm record that the psyche and the in-flight justice system both consume, per-agent last-seen knowledge of things, and a family-stratified top-K menu builder. A scratch prototype of that builder yields 29 options from 282 raw candidates (361 max, which would already exceed JEV's 255 limit) in 0.075 ms, and makes household members targetable 91% of the time. Caveats: all behavioural numbers use the deterministic fake JEV, so they reflect the gating code, not real choices. engine.ts was being edited by another session during this audit (it grew from 3,298 to 3,307 lines), so line numbers may drift by a few.

fundamentals.title: Add a Thing table: every object has a location, owner, durability, contents and a version
fundamentals.problem: No entity or object model exists. Buildings are fixed, immutable records with no owner, hp or contents. Containers are separate one-off structures: one Project, one Pantry, homeFood keyed by building id, and shops keyed by a closed ShopId union. The engine can change tiles in only two ways (burying someone, finishing the bridge). The renderer caches a static layer on the assumption that nothing else changes. Code that looks up a home or workplace throws or asserts non-null. So building a second house, destroying one, opening a new shop, or leaving someone homeless all need new bespoke code, and some would crash today. After the footbridge is finished, the carpenter's job has nothing to build.

fundamentals.proposal: Add World.things: Record<string, Thing>, where Thing = { id, kind: ThingKindId, pos: Vec, size: Vec, holder: {agentId}|{thingId}|null, owner: Owner, access: 'public'|string[], hp, maxHp, state: 'planned'|'building'|'standing'|'damaged'|'ruined', progress, contents: Bundle, coins, builtBy: Record<agentId, units>, business?: Business, version, lastChange: {tick, verb, actorId|null} }. Add a pure THING_KINDS table: { name, blocks, enterable, movable, maxHp, value, recipe: {materials: Bundle, work}, capacity, verbs: VerbId[] }. Maintain a spatial index thingsAt: Map<tileIdx, id[]> and a blocked: Uint8Array overlay that isWalkable consults, rebuilt when a blocking Thing changes. Migrate buildings, pantries, homeFood, shop stock and tills, the project, bushes and graves into Things, keeping hours as a component. homeOf returns Thing|null, and being homeless becomes a valid state (sleep rough).

fundamentals.title: Replace the single food number with item bundles, and make building consume materials
fundamentals.problem: Agent.carry is one number of 'food'. Berries, produce, fish and groceries all merge into it, and selling sells all of it. The only goods are food and coins, so nothing can be gathered as a resource (wood, stone), crafted, or traded by kind. Building consumes time only (sessionsDone += amount), so construction does not tie into gathering or the economy.
fundamentals.evidence: lib/sim/types.ts:331 carry: number ('Food portions carried (berries or fish)'), :332 coins; lib/sim/engine.ts finishWork (farmer and fisher both add to agent.carry, ~515-527); buy adds groceries to carry and sell uses n = min(agent.carry, ...) in arrive (~1810-1835); buildSession :547-560 consumes no materials; docs/society-spec.md:996-1015 already sketches Stack/Store/Owner but it is not implemented
fundamentals.proposal: Add ItemKind = 'berries'|'produce'|'fish'|'groceries'|'meal'|'wood'|'stone'|'tools', with an ITEMS table {hunger, spoilsTicks, weight, baseValue}. Bundle = Partial<Record<ItemKind, number>>. Agent.carry becomes a Bundle with a weight cap. Route every movement of goods or coins through transfer(from: Holder, to: Holder, bundle, coins, mode, byId), where Holder = agent | thing, and extend the existing conservation test to items. THING_KINDS recipes spend materials per work unit from the planned Thing's contents, so anyone can donate materials to a build with put(wood). Material sources are Things: east-woods trees and rock outcrops yield wood or stone into carry, lose hp as they are worked, and regrow. Prices are per (business, item).
fundamentals.unlocks: Gathering resources, construction from materials, production chains, buying and selling by kind, and exploitation or charity over specific goods

fundamentals.title: Make ownership data, and make a generic Harm record the only source of property grievance
fundamentals.problem: No owner field exists anywhere. Who owns what is inferred case by case (Building.residents, Shop.keeperId). What counts as a crime is written inside each verb, so recordCrime('pantry_theft') lives inside arrive(). Grievance is 23 separate nudgeAffinity calls with hand-tuned constants. The crime and life-event lists are closed. So damaging someone's house cannot make them angry unless someone hand-writes that exact consequence. The victim's reaction is a constant, not a choice shaped by their psychology.
fundamentals.evidence: lib/sim/engine.ts nudgeAffinity at 23 sites (grep), e.g. -0.6 murder witness ~1588, -0.15 pantry witness ~1777, -0.35 lie found ~1877, -0.3 default ~2461; engine.ts:1780 recordCrime(world, 'pantry_theft', ...) inline in arrive; lib/sim/types.ts:203 CrimeKind = 'pickpocket'|'pantry_theft'|'assault'|'murder'; lib/sim/drift.ts:86-95 LifeEvent has no property harm; counted 100 remember(), 79 count(world), 54 needs clamps in engine.ts
fundamentals.proposal: Owner = {kind:'agent',id}|{kind:'household',id}|{kind:'group',id}|{kind:'town'}|{kind:'none'}. permission(actor, thing, verb) returns 'own'|'granted'|'public'|'trespass', computed from owner and access. The verb executor emits Harm = { id, tick, verb, actorId, thingId, ownerIds, value (from THING_KINDS.value and the hp or items lost), witnesses, knownBy: {agentId, how:'saw'|'found'|'told', suspectIds}[] } whenever a verb reduces the value of something whose owner is not the actor, without consent. A single onHarmKnown(victim, harm) writes the memory, calls wrongedBy, adds a new lifeEvent 'property_harmed' scaled by value (and more when the victim built it or lives in it), and issues a JEV appraise choice: 'You find the Vale house door smashed; Rook was near it this morning' with options confront | report | retaliate | repair | demand_restitution | let_go. The anger comes from JEV reading the psyche, not from a constant. The in-flight justice system reads Harm through a norm table (verb x permission to crime kind), so vandalism, arson, trespass and property theft become crimes without new justice code.
fundamentals.unlocks: 'Destroy someone's house and they are pissed', revenge and restitution loops, property crimes feeding police cases, generosity measured against real sacrifice

fundamentals.title: Replace bespoke option code with a verb table and one executor
fundamentals.problem: Every behaviour is hand-written across many places. buildOptions is 484 lines. Each intent has cases in 6 switch statements plus ACT_TICKS and the Intent union, and each offer has 3 more switches. A verb like 'deposit' appears 9 times in engine.ts. Children are gated by a regex on option-id prefixes. The spec's ACTIONS table was never built, and it is still one verb per situation (take_<store>, fetch_<store>) rather than generic verbs over objects. Adding destroy, repair, move, claim and build-your-own would mean roughly 9 new code sites per verb.
fundamentals.evidence: lib/sim/engine.ts:1029-1512 buildOptions; switch(intent.kind) at :584 goalFor, :642 happensInside, :682 intentPhrase, :1657 arrive, :1915 finishActing, :2295 applyActing; ACT_TICKS :90-114; types.ts:244 Intent union (27 kinds); engine.ts:1027 ADULT_ONLY regex; grep '"deposit"' = 9 hits in engine.ts; docs/society-spec.md:1749-1770 (unimplemented ActionDef)
fundamentals.proposal: VERBS: Record<VerbId, VerbDef>, where VerbDef = { family: 'body'|'work'|'build'|'property'|'kind'|'hostile'|'civic'|'leisure', target: 'self'|'thing'|'agent'|'thing+item', gate(ctx): physical and knowledge facts only, adultOnly, ticks(ctx), effects(ctx): {needs, transfers, thingDelta}, harm(ctx): Harm|null, drivers(ctx), label(ctx), detail(ctx) with slots What/Where/Effects/Who would know }. There are about 18 generic verbs: eat, drink, sleep, gather, craft, plan, build, repair, damage, demolish, pick_up, place, take, put, give, trade, claim, enter, use (a business's service), plus the existing agent offers. THING_KINDS[k].verbs and Business components say which verbs apply to what. One runVerb(world, agent, verb, target) handles path goal (from the target's door or position), then arrive, then act per tick, then finish. The old switches collapse into it. Keep Intent = {verb, targetId, item?, qty?, params}.
fundamentals.unlocks: Adding a new interaction (break, rearrange, build a fence) becomes one table row. The option text, physics and UI all share one source.

fundamentals.title: Build menus by top-K relevance, with a fixed quota per family
fundamentals.problem: Menus are truncated by fixed rules, not ranked by relevance. Gifts, pleas, loans and pickpocketing are offered only to the single nearest person. Chat goes to the 3 nearest. Hostility goes to the lowest-affinity adult within 8 steps. All 7 explore options appear in every menu. So villagers mostly cannot be kind to family or friends, or confront the person who wronged them without violence, while filler options take up menu space.

Measured (scratch targets.ts, 2,880 ticks, fake JEV): when someone with |affinity|>=0.3 is in sight, none of them is giftable, lendable or complimentable in 544/942 (58%, seed 31) and 419/800 (52%, seed 7) of decisions; household member in sight but none kindness-targetable in 162/200 (81%) and 172/277 (62%); a grudge target in sight has only violence verbs in 42/102 (41%) and 8/13 (62%). Measured menus (scratch menus.ts): p50 30, p90 35, max 52 options; explore averages 7.0 per menu (5,187 over 741 menus)
fundamentals.proposal: enumerate(world, agent): candidates = VERBS x targets. Targets are Things the agent knows (in sight via thingsAt, owned, or in seen memory) and people (in sight, plus household, plus the top 3 by |affinity|, plus grudges and gratitude, plus debt counterparties). Score each candidate from facts only, never traits (the AGENTS.md rule that psychology never ranks options): 1/(1+steps/10), plus need match (the sum of need deficits times the verb's effect on each need), plus |affinity|, plus 0.5 for a grudge or gratitude, plus ownership (own or household), plus salience (the thing's version changed since last seen, or an unresolved Harm), minus a novelty penalty if chosen in the last 6 decisions. Dedupe to one instance per (verb, thing kind, owner class), keeping the best, with at most 2 targets per verb. Fill fixed family quotas (body 5, work 3, build 4, property 4, kind 6, hostile 4, civic 3, leisure 3; total <= 32), so the ratio of prosocial to antisocial options comes from the table, not the situation. Always include rest. Store the scores and what was cut (truncated) on the DecisionRecord. Scratch prototype (affordances.ts, 75 Things from the live world plus 40 trees and 5 movables): raw candidates p50 282, max 361; menu 29; 0.075 ms p50 and 0.56 ms p99 per call, against 0.096 ms for today's buildOptions; a household member in sight is kindness-targetable in 119/131 (91%).
fundamentals.unlocks: Kindness toward chosen people, targeted revenge, bounded and readable JEV menus as the world grows past 255 possible actions, auditable truncation

fundamentals.title: Replace omniscient object state with per-agent last-seen knowledge and discovery
fundamentals.problem: Every villager's perception includes live pantry counts and the status, price and stock of every shop, wherever they are, and option details quote live counts. The only knowledge store is Agent.knows for crimes. Theft discovery is a one-off scalar (missingCoins). For property harm to cause a grievance, the owner has to find out, and must be able to suspect the wrong person. Omniscience would also make the state text grow with every new Thing.
fundamentals.evidence: lib/sim/engine.ts:929-931 placeLine for all three shops in every perception; :958 chapel pantry count always; :1241 option detail quotes live pantry food; :1002 noticing.slice(0, 32); lib/sim/types.ts:337 missingCoins, :351 knows (crimes only). Measured (scratch state.ts): state text p50 3,518 chars, p90 4,040; noticing lines p50 17, max 27
fundamentals.proposal: Add Agent.seen: Record<thingId, {v, tick, hp, contents?: Bundle, price?}>, refreshed whenever a Thing is in sight or the agent is inside it. Perception and verb labels read from seen (stated as last seen at <time>), never live state. On arrival, verbs re-check real state and cancel with a memory if it differs. If an agent sees a Thing they own whose version has advanced and a Harm they don't yet know about, discovery fires onHarmKnown with how = 'found' and suspects = the people this agent saw near it during that window. The suspects can be wrong. The perception shows owned Things (state plus last change), Things in sight, and the top 5 remembered by salience, so the text stays bounded.
fundamentals.unlocks: Finding out about vandalism or theft, wrong accusations, rumours and gossip about property, legible state text as the world grows

fundamentals.title: Make construction, destruction, repair and rearranging physics that change function
fundamentals.problem: Given Things and items, the verbs still need consequences that come from world state rather than hand-written text. Today the only lasting world changes are graves and a finished bridge, and a building's function (home, shop, clinic) never depends on its condition.
fundamentals.evidence: lib/sim/engine.ts:1892-1913 completeProject (the only build outcome, flips tiles to 'bridge'); :547-560 buildSession; world-canvas.tsx:251-255 static cache invalidated only on graves.length; step() already cancels a move when the next tile is unwalkable (engine.ts moving case, 'if (!isWalkable(...)) becomeIdle')
fundamentals.proposal: plan: on a free lot or free tiles, offer the top 2 buildable kinds x 2 nearest free sites. This creates Thing{state:'planned'}, owned by the planner (or by the town or a group when planned at the town hall). build: spends recipe materials from the Thing's contents plus work units, and credits builtBy. damage: hp drops by effort times tools. demolish: at hp 0 the state becomes 'ruined' and the contents spill into a pile Thing that stays owned by the original owner, so taking from it is theft. repair: materials restore hp. pick_up and place: move movable Things (bench, crate, fence segment), updating the blocked overlay; in-flight paths already fail safely. Function follows state: a damaged home restores less energy and leaves its food unsecured; a ruined home makes its residents homeless; a ruined business cannot serve. Each change bumps a world.thingsVersion that the canvas uses to redraw its Things layer.
fundamentals.unlocks: Rearranging the village, building homes and fences, sabotage and repair, visible long-term traces of what people did

fundamentals.title: Attach businesses and workplaces to Things instead of fixed building kinds
fundamentals.problem: Institutions are hardwired one per building kind, so villagers cannot organize anything new: no second shop, no market stall run by a group, no co-owned shed. Jobs resolve their workplace with buildingOf(kind)!. The shops are a closed three-key record, each selling one good at one price.

summary: Fernhollow has none of the primitives self-organization needs. There are no collectives, memberships, shared purses, proposals, votes, rules or elected offices, and no beliefs that pass from one mind to another. Every social act is between two people and the target is picked by distance: gifts, loans, pleas and pickpocketing go only to the single nearest person outdoors, and people sitting together inside the Lantern, diner or chapel can never address each other. In real JEV records, 88-95% of approaches went to the nearest person, even though JEV put 31-41% of its probability on approaching someone. So the missing groups, alliances, reputations and norms are not JEV declining to choose them: the option space cannot express them. The spec designs much of this (Slice B, M6/M7/M17/M19), but it splits it into town-only ordinances and clubs that are little more than labels; the fix is one generic Collective + Proposal/Meeting/Vote + Rule-as-data trio that the town, households and emergent groups all instantiate. Add to that a belief store so opinions travel, and "whom" as its own JEV choice. Pilot, per the dogfood rule: ship the whom-choice and talking to people in the same building first. Then make the chapel pantry the first commons its users govern: any member can call a chapel meeting, propose a take-limit rule, attendees vote, and violations feed the in-flight Case system. Run 2-3 real JEV days; it passes if at least one rule is proposed and adopted by vote and at least one violation is reported under it. (Line numbers refer to the working tree at about 20:00 on 2026-09-23, which a parallel agent is still editing.)

fundamentals.title: Let villagers choose whom, and talk to whoever is in the room
fundamentals.problem: Person-directed options are built from distance alone. Talk goes to the 3 nearest people who can be approached. Compliment, gift, lend, plea, lie and pickpocket go only to the single nearest one. Violence is the exception: it targets the least-liked adult within 8 steps. So hatred can choose its target, but love, loyalty and alliance cannot. canApproach excludes anyone inside a building, and a chase is abandoned when the target goes indoors. The Lantern, diner, chapel and town hall, the natural places for groups to form, therefore put people in the same room without letting them interact.
fundamentals.evidence: engine.ts:879-881 canApproach returns !target.inside; engine.ts:1257-1260 approachable.slice(0, TALK_OPTIONS=3); engine.ts:1281 `const nearest = approachable[0]` gates give/lend/ask/lie/usury/pickpocket; engine.ts:1441 foe = least-liked within 8 steps; engine.ts:2200 chase gives up when the target goes inside. Measured in real-JEV lab records (seed 600, ticks before the desync): 63 of 72 and 100 of 105 chosen approaches went to the nearest person, while approach options held 31% and 41% of JEV's probability. Fake JEV, 5 seeds x 7 days: at most 1 transfer target per decision, and the most-liked person was the gift target in only 9.5% of gift-offering decisions. Indoor test: Hollis, inside the Rusty Lantern with Lark and Mo listed as 'here with you', got 10 person options, all aimed at people outside (talk_bram, pickpocket_bram, attack_bram and others).
fundamentals.proposal: Collapse the per-person duplicate options into one option per act with a placeholder target, for example 'Give 1 food to someone', 'Lend 5 coins to someone', 'Go talk to someone', 'Say something kind to someone', 'Pick someone's pocket', 'Attack someone'. When JEV picks one, issue a follow-up `whom` choice call conditioned on that act. Its criteria are every living person the chooser knows (255 at most), each labelled with relationship and location, e.g. 'Mo (cook): you like her; she helped you twice this week; last seen at the diner 20 min ago, 14 steps'. Add `Intent.seek {offer, targetId}`, which walks to the person's believed location and falls back to the existing giveUpTalk. Change canApproach so a person in the same building as the asker counts (reuse canSee). Keep today's nearest-person default only as the fallback when a whom call fails. Cost: one extra call, only on person-directed picks (about 30% of decisions), at the measured ~$0.0001 each.
fundamentals.unlocks: Being kind to a specific person, favouritism, reciprocity, alliances and in-group bias, with revenge and loyalty on an equal footing. Recruiting members (Collective) and canvassing votes (Meetings) both depend on it. It also frees about 8-10 option slots under the 64-option cap.

fundamentals.title: A belief layer: perception reads what you know, and talk carries claims
fundamentals.problem: Minds read the world's true state directly, and no information passes between minds. Every perception carries six world-level facts wherever the villager is standing: the exact pantry count, the footbridge percentage with its full contributor list, all three shops' status and prices, and the berries. A chat carries no content: it adds social need and +0.1 liking. Knowledge of crimes (Agent.knows, a list of crime ids) spreads only by eyewitness, a report to the officer, or the Crier. The Crier's headlines come from a regex over the journalist's memories, not from her choice. So opinions cannot spread, reputations cannot form or be manipulated, and nobody can recruit anyone. It also breaks the spec's own rule that reputation exists only in beliefs and ties: the engine broadcasts who built the bridge to everyone.
fundamentals.evidence: engine.ts:929-931 and 958-964 are the global lines; engine.ts:863-867 contributorsPhrase; the chat tick at engine.ts:2572-2580 and applyChatReply at 3055 (a yes/no engage question only, prompt.ts respondQuestions); printEdition regex at engine.ts:563-579. Measured over 4229 decisions: 6 global-state lines in every perception (minimum 6). Each crime was known to 22% of the living on average, 43% at p90. In the real replays the oldest memory shown to JEV was a median 4-5 hours old (MEMORY_IN_PROMPT=7), so anything learned in the morning is gone by evening unless it is stored as a record.
fundamentals.proposal: World.beliefs, indexed by holder: `Belief = { id, holderId, about: {kind: 'agent'|'collective'|'store'|'project'|'rule', id}, claim: 'did_crime'|'broke_rule'|'helped'|'pledged'|'defaulted'|'member_of'|'holds_office'|'store_level'|'supports'|'meeting_at', ref, source: 'saw'|{toldBy}|'read_board', credence: 0..1, tick }`. `perceive` renders public facts from the holder's beliefs, with their age ('when you last looked, Tue 3 pm, the pantry held 4'), and sight refreshes those beliefs. Chat gets a topic: when a chat starts, the speaker answers a `topic` choice over up to 8 salient beliefs, plus 'small talk', plus 'make up something about X' (tagged with the deception driver). The listener answers `believe` in the same reply call, a 0-4 score mapped to credence as EV/4, and the belief is copied with its source chain. `knows` becomes a view over did_crime beliefs, so the in-flight justice code keeps working and reports can be hearsay with a credence. The journalist's edition becomes a JEV choice over her own beliefs.
fundamentals.unlocks: Opinions spreading, gossip, reputation, manipulation and propaganda, recruiting into groups, and calling meetings by word of mouth. It also gives 'destroy someone's house and their friends are angry too' its path, and makes the Crier matter.

fundamentals.title: Collective as a first-class record: the town, households and groups are the same thing
fundamentals.problem: Nothing bigger than one person has a record. There are no groups, no membership, no roles, no shared purse and no gathering schedule. The town is a bundle of globals (treasury, taxRate, worked) that nobody controls. The spec's Group type (club, union, congregation or crew, with a purse and a weekly gathering) has no rules, dues or meetings of its own. Rules and votes live only in town-hall Ordinance and Meeting records, so only the town can make rules. That is institutions handed down, not self-organization.
fundamentals.evidence: types.ts World has no groups or collectives, and Town is only {treasury, taxRate, worked}. Spec lines 1155-1163: Group has no ruleIds, dues or meetings. Spec lines 1064-1069: Meeting and Ordinance exist only for the town. Spec M19 at 2265-2284.
fundamentals.proposal: `Collective = { id, kind: 'town'|'household'|'club'|'crew'|'congregation'|'union', name (a choice among 4 seeded names per kind), parentId (the town, for nesting), members: Record<agentId, {since, role: 'member'|'leader'|officeId}>, purse: {food, coins}, home: buildingId|poiId, gathering: {weekday, minute}|null, ruleIds, foundedBy, foundedTick }`. The town's purse is the treasury. World creation makes only c_town (every resident) and one household collective per home; every other collective has to be founded. Options are generated from these records, not from code branches: `found_<kind>` (a talk offer; a yes reply makes the listener the first member), `invite_<cid>` and `ask_join_<cid>` (answered by the leader or any member present), `leave_<cid>`, `give_to_<cid>`, `take_from_<cid>` (witnessed and checked against its rules), and `attend_<cid>` at gathering time. Perception gets one line per membership: size, leader, purse, and what its rules ask of you this week.
fundamentals.unlocks: Groups forming, factions, self-organization, pooled resources, shared treasuries and nesting (Ostrom's principle 8). Groups get meetings, rules and projects from the same code as the town.

fundamentals.title: Proposals, meetings and votes as the one collective-choice procedure
fundamentals.problem: No villager can call a meeting, propose anything, vote or elect. The only collective project was approved before tick 0. The mayor's job is flavour: an hour at the town hall adds respect +3. The tax rate is a constant, and the mayor and officer hold office by persona data forever. Collective choice, the step that turns many preferences into shared state, is missing.
fundamentals.evidence: engine.ts:535-537, the mayor's work case (respect only); SALES_TAX is a constant at engine.ts:84, applied once at 241; personas.ts:394 'Tomas appointed you chief of police.'; the project is fixed at engine.ts:223-232; types.ts has no meeting or vote types; spec M6 (2026-2067) designs these only for the town hall.
fundamentals.proposal: `Proposal = { id, collectiveId, kind: 'adopt_rule'|'repeal_rule'|'elect'|'spend'|'start_project'|'admit'|'expel'|'set_dues'|'dissolve', params, proposerId, meetingId, status }` and `Meeting = { id, collectiveId, calledBy, place, tick, agenda, attendees, ballot: 'open'|'secret', votes: Record<proposalId, Record<agentId, string>> }`. A pure `proposalCatalog(world, collective, proposer)` lists concrete typed items, capped at 255: rule templates with 2-3 parameter values each, candidates for each office, spend amounts per project. Any member can pick `call_meeting_<cid>` and then answers an `agenda` choice over the catalog (1-2 items), so JEV never writes rule text. The meeting becomes a notice at the collective's place and a meeting_at belief for anyone present or told. When it starts, members who are there enter a `meeting` status, and each attendee gets one `vote` call per item (yes/no/abstain, or candidates plus abstain). Under an open ballot the calls run in sequence and each voter's state lists the declarations made before theirs. A majority of attendees decides, with a quorum of ceil(members/3), and a pure `enact(world, proposal)` applies the result. The town's weekly meeting is simply c_town's gathering. Cost: 10 attendees x 2 items = 20 calls, about $0.002. At the measured median latency of 250 ms, an open ballot takes about 2.5 s.
fundamentals.unlocks: Town meetings and voting, elections, collective action, spending from a purse, expulsion and banishment, and legitimacy experiments. It also makes herding under open ballots measurable.

fundamentals.title: Rules as data that agents see, obey or break, and justice enforces
fundamentals.problem: What counts as wrong is written into the engine, not chosen by anyone. CrimeKind is a fixed union. 'Pantry theft' is defined by the engine's own need test (hunger under 30, or unable to afford groceries), and the same test sets the option's driver tag. Fines are constants per crime kind. Nobody can make a rule (a pantry limit, curfew, price cap, dues), so there can be no norms, no one pushing for new norms, no breaking of a rule the town itself chose, and no norms changing over time. The in-flight justice system therefore enforces the programmer's laws.
fundamentals.evidence: types.ts:203 CrimeKind; engine.ts:1243 and 1766 apply the need test; engine.ts:1780 records pantry_theft; engine.ts:1413 hard-codes fine amounts; Ordinance and SanctionLevel exist only in the spec (lines 1067-1068).
fundamentals.proposal: `Rule = { id, collectiveId, template, params, sanction: 0..4 (warn, fine, repay double, night in the cell, expel or banish), adoptedBy: proposalId|'county', adoptedTick, status }`, drawn from a fixed catalog of about 40 templates or fewer: take_limit(storeId, n per day), members_only(storeId), need_only(storeId), dues(kind, n per week), work_levy(projectId, hours per week), price_cap(good, max), curfew(hour), no_theft, no_violence, attend_gathering, tax_rate(pct), banish(agentId). A pure `violations(world, actor, act): Rule[]` runs wherever an act resolves (arrive, applyResponse). A violation creates the in-flight Crime with `kind: {rule: ruleId}`, plus beliefs for witnesses ('you saw Hollis take a second portion; the town voted a one-a-day limit on Thursday'). Option details say it honestly: 'This breaks the town's pantry rule (sanction: a fine)'. Case options for the officer or a collective's monitor are generated from known violations, and the sanction ladder comes from the rule. Murder, assault and theft stay in force as rules adopted by 'county', so the in-flight work stays valid.
fundamentals.unlocks: Norms and sanctions; rules agents can see, vote on, obey or break; justice enforcing law the town made itself; Ostrom's principles 2, 3 and 5; game-theory experiments on compliance versus enforcement.

fundamentals.title: Offices as seats that can be vacated, contested and filled
fundamentals.problem: Institutional roles are welded to persona.job, which nothing ever reassigns. The officer is found as the living person whose job is police_officer, and the store opens only while its fixed keeper is inside. With murder now in flight, one death can permanently disable justice or the town's only grocery. There is no election, appointment, succession, deputy or removal from office, so leadership cannot emerge or be contested.
fundamentals.evidence: engine.ts:1519 officerOf; engine.ts:1386 gates case options on persona.job; engine.ts:347 shopOpen requires the fixed keeperId; no code anywhere assigns persona.job (grep). Measured with fake JEV, seed 7: after killing Odile and Sable at tick 5, the next 4 days had 30 crimes, 0 decisions offering a report or case option, 0 cases and 0 store purchases.
fundamentals.proposal: `Office = { id, collectiveId, title, holderId|null, powers: ('open_case'|'arrest'|'fine'|'set_agenda'|'spend_purse_upto'|'appoint_acting'|'keep_store'|'set_price')[], term|null, since, filledBy: proposalId|'founding' }`. Every power-gated option checks `holds(world, agent, power)` instead of persona.job; persona.job only seeds the first holder. Death, jail, leaving town or a `resign_<office>` option empties the seat, and `elect(office)` is added to the collective's next meeting agenda automatically. An office with appoint_acting lets its holder name a stand-in through a whom choice. Groups create their own offices (leader, treasurer, monitor) by proposal.
fundamentals.unlocks: Leadership, elections, succession after a murder, abuse of office and legitimacy. It also lets the justice system survive the violence it now makes possible.

fundamentals.title: Commons governed by their users (Ostrom)
fundamentals.problem: The chapel pantry and the berry bushes are open to all, with etiquette the engine defines. Anyone may take 2 per trip, 'meant for those in need' is only prose, the engine decides who is in need, and monitoring is whoever happens to be in the chapel. There is no collective choice about access, no ledger, no graduated sanction and no monitor. The berries have no rule at all, and the treasury is a commons nobody can spend. Every Ostrom design principle needs the Collective, Rule, Meeting and Office primitives. Without them a tragedy of the commons, or its avoidance, can only be scripted, never emerge.
fundamentals.evidence: engine.ts:1239-1245 take_store option; engine.ts:1762-1790 take physics with the engine's need test; engine.ts:2368 regrowBerries has no access control; the treasury moves only through payroll and deliveries in townDay (engine.ts:2377).
fundamentals.proposal: Every shared store becomes `Store { id, ownerCollectiveId, food, coins, ledger: {tick, agentId, delta}[] }`: the pantry is owned by c_town or a founded congregation, and each grove of bushes is a store owned by c_town. Access goes through rules (take_limit, members_only, need_only). The ledger can be read at the store (a read_ledger option creates store_level and took beliefs), and that is the monitoring. A monitor office gets case options for violations it knows about. Sanctions follow the rule's ladder and escalate with repeat offences. This is the first vertical slice to build and dogfood on the Collective, Meeting, Rule and Office primitives.
fundamentals.unlocks: Governed shared resources (Ostrom), measurable free-riding, and self-organization around scarcity (the famine intervention becomes a test of governance). It also brings treasury politics.

fundamentals.title: Projects proposed, funded and pledged, not pre-approved
fundamentals.problem: The footbridge is the only collective action, and it was approved before tick 0. The world holds one Project, contributions take no inputs (no wood, coins or pooled resources), and once it is finished nothing can ever be built again. Help is asked of individuals hour by hour with no commitment, so free-riding, pledges, broken promises and claiming credit cannot happen. In real runs the paid carpenter did most of the work.
fundamentals.evidence: World.project is a single record (types.ts), created at engine.ts:223-232 with BRIDGE_SESSIONS=16 (engine.ts:88); completeProject at engine.ts:1892; the build option at engine.ts:1206 is gated on the bridge being unfinished. Measured with fake JEV: after completion (3 of 5 seeds, at ticks 1141-1901), 0 of 551 decisions offered a build option. In real runs, Wren (the paid carpenter) did 6 of 7 and 5 of 9 sessions, and building/justice/duty options outside work got 2.0% and 2.6% of the probability.
fundamentals.proposal: `projects: Project[]` drawn from a template catalog (footbridge, well, shed, a house on lot_a or lot_b, fence, bandstand, memorial). Each has `inputs {sessions, coins, wood}`, a `sponsorId` (a collective or an agent) and `pledges: Commitment[]`, with `Commitment = {id, promiserId, projectId, amount, dueTick, status: 'open'|'kept'|'broken'}` (the spec already declares it). A project starts through a start_project or spend proposal, or privately with the founder's own coins. A `pledge_<project>` option (a choice of amount) creates a commitment shown in perception ('You pledged 2 hours on the well by Friday; you have given 0'). A broken pledge creates beliefs among the collective's members. The global contributor broadcast is replaced by beliefs.
fundamentals.unlocks: Building things, collective action, pooling resources, providing, credit and blame, free-rider game theory, and rearranging the village.

fundamentals.title: Ties with memory: a visible favours ledger and relationships JEV appraises
fundamentals.problem: A relationship is one number moved by 23 hard-coded nudges (+0.1 per chat, -0.6 for an attack, -0.5 for a pickpocket), so feuds and alliances are the engine's arithmetic rather than anyone's judgement. The favours ledger that would let a villager reason 'Mo has helped me three times; I owe her' is recorded but read only by metrics. Perception shows at most 8 feelings lines and 7 memories covering about 5 hours. Third parties never react: harm done to your kin or a fellow member reaches you only if you saw it.
fundamentals.evidence: engine.ts:286 nudgeAffinity (23 call sites); favours are written at engine.ts:291-296 and read only in metrics.ts:200 and digest.ts:26; feelings at engine.ts:1007-1014; MEMORY_IN_PROMPT=7 at engine.ts:66; measured memory horizon is a median 4-5 hours in the real replays.
fundamentals.proposal: `Tie = { liking, trust, respect, balance (favours given minus received), lastSeen: {place, tick} }` for each directed pair, rendered as people lines: 'Mo: you like and trust her; she has helped you 3 times this week and you have not returned it; last seen at the diner'. After salient events, replace the fixed nudges with a JEV `feel` score (0-4, mapped by EV) asked on the affected person's next call. That includes third parties who hear about it through a belief concerning someone they are tied to or share a collective with. Add the spec's nightly tie_level appraisal for up to 2 people, so small changes stop piling up.
fundamentals.unlocks: Reciprocity, alliances, feuds, and 'destroy someone's house and they, their family and their group are angry'. Also in-group bias.

fundamentals.title: Kinship and real households
fundamentals.problem: 11 of 12 households have one person; the Harrows are the only family. There is no kin record in code (the spec's Kin type is only on paper). So Mo being Pip's sibling, inheritance, family feuds, providing for family, and the household as the first collective are all missing. Stocking the home pantry counts as help only for people who live there.
fundamentals.evidence: Measured households: b_inn:1, h_vale:1 and nine more single homes, h_harrow:4 (town-map.ts:197-224). types.ts has no kin; spec sections 3.5 (lines 468-482) and 954-962 describe it; engine.ts:1721 credits help only to co-residents.
fundamentals.proposal: `Agent.kin: Record<agentId, 'partner'|'parent'|'child'|'sibling'>`, seeded from spec 3.5. Households become Collectives of kind household, with the home pantry as the purse. Perception adds lines about dependents ('Kit is hungry; your pantry holds 2'). An `invite_to_live` offer changes membership and moves residence. On a death, possessions and business deeds go to the household collective. Partnership and children belong to the family lens and can build on this.
fundamentals.unlocks: Providing for family, loyalty to kin, feuds over inheritance, households organizing themselves (moving in, pooling food), and reproduction later.

summary: Fernhollow's villagers have a detailed psyche but very little cognition. Memory is a 14-entry text queue (oldest dropped first) with only the last 7 entries shown to JEV. Each villager has one liking number per person, moved by 23 hard-coded constants. Nothing records who believes what or where they heard it. Emotion does not persist: mood is asked on every call and never read back. There are no intentions: every finished action becomes a fresh choice among about 26 options, while the engine quietly commits villagers to walks and chases that can last hours. Measured: villagers facing someone recall their past with that person less over time (0.68 over 3 days, 0.58 over 10). The other person's relationship line is missing in 38% of reply calls. Salient events drop out of the prompt in about 9 hours. Reflection is keyed to the calendar day, so in the real 15-villager run 5 people reflected twice, once at bedtime and again at midnight, and their next day never gets its own reflection. These gaps block "destroy someone's house and they will be pissed", gossip and spreading opinions, targeted revenge or kindness, providing for family, and self-organization. JEV cannot write text, so the right design is structured state rendered into template text, with JEV acting as the rater and chooser: a memory stream scored by importance and relevance where JEV rates importance, relationships and sourced beliefs that JEV updates through feel and believe scores, emotions from appraisal that fade over time, daily intentions chosen from template aims and reconsidered only when something happens, and "who" sub-questions so the villager, not proximity, picks the target. Cost is not the constraint (measured at about $0.0001 per call). The data model should land before the persistent live world builds up long-lived state, because the checkpoint loader only fills in missing fields.

fundamentals.title: A memory stream scored by importance and relevance (replace the 14-entry queue)
fundamentals.problem: A memory is only {tick, text}. It has no kind, no participants, no importance and no event link. The engine keeps 14, drops the oldest first, and shows JEV the last 7. There are 99 remember() call sites and every memory counts the same, so routine lines crowd out salient ones. When a villager is facing someone, the memories JEV sees are the most recent, not the ones about that person. Reflection reads at most the last 10. Over a long-running persistent world this gets steadily worse.
fundamentals.evidence: lib/sim/types.ts:308 (MemoryEntry); engine.ts:65-66 (MEMORY_KEEP=14, MEMORY_IN_PROMPT=7), engine.ts:268-271 (push/shift), engine.ts:1005 (slice(-7)), engine.ts:2434 (reflection gets .slice(-10)). Measured with the needs-sensible heuristic: 63% of memories are routine (beat walks, woke up, rest, drink). With the random fake over 3 days: salient memories (attacked, robbed, lied to, death, arrest) stay in the prompt for a median 565 min (p90 810) and in the buffer for a median 730 min. Recall of any non-chat past with the person you are facing: 0.68 over 3 days, 0.58 over 10 days (86/126 and 286/490 reply calls). Real run s600: Odile's memory held 'You walked your beat around town' four times out of 11 entries.
fundamentals.proposal: type Memory = { id: string; tick: number; text: string; kind: 'routine'|'social'|'work'|'money'|'kindness'|'wrong_to_you'|'wrong_by_you'|'violence'|'loss'|'news'|'justice'; about: string[] /*agent ids*/; place: string|null; eventId: string|null; importance: number /*0..1*/; formative: boolean; recalled: number }. remember(world, agent, text, {kind, about, eventId}) sets a starting importance from kind (routine .05, social .2, money .4, kindness .5, wrong_to_you .8, violence .9, loss 1.0). For starting importance >= 0.5, the villager's next call carries an extra appraise_<memId> score question ('How hard does this hit {name}?', 5 levels), and importance = EV/4. Keep up to 300 per agent, evicting the lowest-scoring non-formative memory. retrieve(agent, focus, k) scores each memory as 0.995^ageHours + importance + relevance, where relevance is 1 if about overlaps focus.people (people in view, the asker or target, option targets, the current intention's target) and 0.3 if the place matches. The prompt shows 3 formative memories, the top 5 retrieved and the last 4 routine memories, with repeats collapsed ('You walked your beat 4 times this afternoon'). Reply and violence calls set focus to the other person. This is Park et al.'s retrieval, using structured ids instead of embeddings.
fundamentals.unlocks: 'destroy their house and they are pissed' days later, lasting grudges and gratitude, reciprocity, revenge, and coherent long-running persistent worlds; also the base for beliefs, emotions and reflection insights

fundamentals.title: Relationships and sourced beliefs updated by JEV, and chats that carry content
fundamentals.problem: Each relationship is one liking number from -1 to 1, changed by fixed constants chosen by the engine, so the engine decides how a villager feels. The 'how you feel about others' section is the top 8 by strength, with no reasons, and it is dominated by the starting relationships. Knowledge of wrongdoing is a list of crime ids that is ground truth, never uncertain or sourced. Chats carry nothing: the only effects are +0.1 liking and a memory line. So opinions cannot spread, there is no reputation, and the three stores (memory text, crime ids, liking) disagree. Example: Mo was offered 'Report Hollis' (she knows crime_8), but her memories and feelings said nothing about Hollis.
fundamentals.evidence: types.ts:351 (knows), types.ts:356 (affinity); 23 nudgeAffinity call sites in engine.ts, e.g. :2151 (-0.5 for a noticed pickpocket), :1775 (-0.15 for pantry witnesses), :2578 (+0.1 after a chat), :2977 (-0.3/-0.6 after an attack); engine.ts:1007-1010 (feelings = top 8 by |affinity|); engine.ts:1541 (recordCrime pushes ground truth to knowers); engine.ts:3055 and :2577 (a chat transfers nothing). Measured with the random fake, 3 seeds x 3 days: the asker's feelings line was missing in 98 of 257 reply calls (38%), including 12 of 25 attack replies and 4 of 4 demands to repay. After 3 days, 5.54 of the 8 feelings lines were still at their starting values and 74 of 210 pairs had changed. docs/society-spec.md:541 already says to retire the fixed nudges; it has not been done in lib/sim.
fundamentals.proposal: type Tie = { liking: number; trust: number; fear: number; familiarity: number; lastSeen: { tick: number; place: string; doing: string } | null; why: string[] /* top 2 memory ids by importance */ }. type Belief = { id: string; claim: 'took_from'|'hurt'|'killed'|'lied_to'|'destroyed'|'helped'|'owes'|'gouges'|'is_kind'|'is_dangerous'; actorId: string; targetId: string|null; eventId: string|null; source: { kind: 'saw'|'told'|'crier'|'reflection'; fromId?: string }; credence: number; tick: number }. Replace the fixed constants with extra questions on the affected villager's next call: feel_<otherId> scores 'How does {name} feel about {other} now, compared with before?' on 5 levels, and liking += 0.1*(EV-2)*(0.5+importance). trust_<id> works the same way. Chat gains content: the asker answers topic, a choice over up to 4 beliefs with credence >= 0.5 plus small_talk, and the listener answers believe, a 5-level score, which creates a Belief with source told and credence = f(EV, trust in the asker). Lies become false beliefs planted this way. Render each relationship with its reasons: 'Hollis: you dislike him; you saw him pick Juniper's pocket (yesterday); Mo says he cheats (you half believe it).' The person addressing you is always listed first. The knowledge lists become views over Beliefs.
fundamentals.unlocks: gossip, spreading opinions, reputation, groups forming around shared beliefs and liking, manipulation and deception of specific people, kindness that is noticed and talked about, and informed revenge or justice

fundamentals.title: Intentions that persist, reconsidered only when something happens (replacing blind engine commitments)
fundamentals.problem: Every finished action ends in becomeIdle and a fresh choice among about 26 options, so nothing carries over from one decision to the next. A shift is re-decided every hour and competes each time with 25 alternatives. The life goal is only a sentence in the psyche section, with no steps toward it. At the same time, the engine commits villagers without asking them: a chase lasts up to 50 ticks, and walks cannot be interrupted, so villagers cannot react to what happens on the way.
fundamentals.evidence: engine.ts:2043 (finishActing then becomeIdle); engine.ts:97 (work = TICKS_PER_HOUR, one decision per hour); engine.ts:995-996 (goal is just a psyche line); engine.ts:63 and :2215 (CHASE_GIVE_UP_TICKS=50). Real run fernhollow-founders-s600-20260923233212 (raw events): 268 decisions with a mean top-option probability of 0.49 (25.8 options on average in the replay), so each hour is effectively re-rolled. Replay trace: Odile (police officer, shift 8 am to 8 pm) picked talk_tomas at 7:55 and chased him until 11:15 (40 ticks) without being asked again, missing 3h20m of her shift. Needs-sensible heuristic over 3 days: 74% of awake ticks spent moving, median trip 21 tiles (105 in-game minutes), only 4 chats. Shift attendance in the real runs was 0.36 to 0.40.
fundamentals.proposal: type Intention = { id: string; aim: AimKey; targetId?: string; steps: Intent[]; step: number; since: number; until: number; why: string|null /* memory or belief id */; shared: string[] }; agent.intention: Intention|null. A new plan call runs on waking and whenever an intention finishes or fails. It asks aim, a choice over up to 20 aims built from templates using affordances, the life goal and current beliefs ('Work your full shift at the clinic', 'Get even with Hollis for what he did', 'Finish the footbridge with Wren', 'Put food on the table for Pip', 'Keep to yourself today', 'Find someone to court'), and until, a score over time horizons. Each later decide shows 'Your plan: {aim} (step 2 of 3, since 8 am)' and a first option continue_plan that shows the next step, but the villager can still choose something else. Work becomes a single intent that runs until the shift ends. The engine emits typed interrupts: being attacked or addressed, a crime within witness range, being named in the Crier, the body alarm crossing a threshold, a chase target going inside, a plan step becoming impossible, or someone important coming into view. An interrupt triggers a cheap reconsider yes/no call: '{name} is {doing}. {interrupt}. Does {name} stop?' Chases reconsider every 12 ticks instead of the fixed give-up. A new recruit offer ('Wren asks you to help build the footbridge this afternoon') adds the listener to shared on acceptance.
fundamentals.unlocks: multi-step behaviour for purpose, building and providing for family, revenge plans, self-organization through shared intentions, reactions to events, and fewer routine calls

fundamentals.title: Emotions from appraisal that persist and fade
fundamentals.problem: Emotion has no state. Mood is asked on every call and written to agent.mood, but perception and physics never read it; only the UI and the digest do. Grief is recorded in a list nobody reads. The engine assigns grief by rule and applies a one-time -20 to social and fun. Anger is folded into the liking number, and fear, shame, guilt and pride do not exist. JEV therefore re-infers each villager's mood from scratch on every call, mainly from the needs text.
fundamentals.evidence: lib/jev/prompt.ts:103-117, :348, :390 (mood asked in decide, reflect and violence calls); engine.ts:2677, :3138 (agent.mood written, with no read in perceive, engine.ts:903-1017); engine.ts:1580-1585 (engine-assigned grief), types.ts:353 (grieving, write-only). Across all 9 recorded real runs with motive readouts there is no 'grievance' motive at all.
fundamentals.proposal: type Emotion = { kind: 'anger'|'fear'|'grief'|'shame'|'guilt'|'pride'|'gratitude'|'joy'; towardId: string|null; intensity: number /*0..1*/; since: number; memoryId: string }. It is created by an extra appraise question on the affected villager's next call, for memories with importance >= 0.5: emotion, a choice over the kinds that fit the event, and intensity, a 5-level score. Intensity fades exponentially with a half-life set by the psyche: high neuroticism slows the fading of fear and anger, high agreeableness speeds up the fading of anger, and grief has a base half-life of about 7 days. Perception gets a new section, 'How you feel inside', with at most 4 lines ('You are still angry at Hollis for picking your pocket (since yesterday morning)'). Emotions adjust needRates (grief multiplies the social and fun drain by 1.5; fear makes security matter more), which stays within the rule that psychology works only through words, rates and consequences. Either drop mood from decide or keep it only as a measurement.
fundamentals.unlocks: 'that person is going to be pissed', grief after a murder, guilt and shame after a crime, pride after building, and revenge or kindness driven by emotion that differs by psyche

fundamentals.title: Reflect once per sleep cycle, not per calendar day, and store insights
fundamentals.problem: Reflection fires on any sleeping tick where the calendar day has changed since the last one. Sleeping across midnight therefore triggers a second reflection at 0:00, and a daytime nap uses up that day's reflection early. The helpers and wrongers lists reset at midnight, so a reflection after midnight never sees them. The drift cap is also per calendar day, so a double reflection gets two caps. Reflection outputs are menus (change, goal) plus grudge or gratitude over today's wrongers only. It stores no conclusion about anyone, unlike Park et al.'s reflection, which writes insights back into memory.
fundamentals.evidence: engine.ts:2584-2585 (lastReflectDay !== today), engine.ts:2486 (today reset at midnight), engine.ts:2434 (memories from the same day or the last 144 ticks, last 10), drift.ts:40-43 (daily cap by calendar day). Real run fernhollow-founders-s600-20260923233212, 15 agents, one night: 17 reflections, 6 of them exactly at day 2, 0:00. Five agents reflected twice (Ivy at 21:10 and 0:00, Wren at 23:00 and 0:00, Sable at 23:15 and 0:00, Pip at 20:00 and 0:00, Bram at 22:00 and 0:00). Needs-sensible heuristic over 3 days: 45 reflections at times from 0:00 to 13:05; the midnight ones had 0 memories from that day. drift-models-engine-habits: reflections at 9:25, 12:15 and 14:25 (naps).
fundamentals.proposal: Replace lastReflectDay with lastReflectTick. Reflect on the first sleep that starts at least 16 hours after the last reflection, or after 7 pm. The payload is memories since lastReflectTick ranked by importance, not the last 10. Helpers and wrongers cover the period since the last reflection instead of resetting at midnight. Add insight_<personId> for the 2 people with the highest importance today: a choice over template conclusions ('{X} cannot be trusted', '{X} is a true friend', '{X} takes advantage of people', '{X} is dangerous', 'nothing new about {X}'). It creates a Belief with source reflection and a memory that can become formative. Add forgive, a choice over existing grudges plus nobody (already in the spec).
fundamentals.unlocks: correct evolution of traits and drift, grudges and forgiveness that build up over days, and the higher-level opinions that let groups and reputations form

fundamentals.title: Let villagers choose whom: 'who' sub-questions instead of proximity targeting
fundamentals.problem: The engine picks every social target. Only the 3 nearest people can be chatted with. Every gift, loan, request, lie and pickpocket goes only to the single nearest person. Violence is offered only against the lowest-liked adult within 8 tiles, and killing only if there is a grudge or liking is at or below -0.4. When a victim flees, the engine sends them home with a 'stock the pantry' intent. As a result a villager cannot provide for a loved one who is not the closest person, and cannot target a specific enemy.
fundamentals.evidence: engine.ts:69 (TALK_OPTIONS=3), :1257-1260 (the nearest approachable people), :1281 (const nearest = approachable[0] receives every transactional offer), :1441 (foe = lowest liking within 8), :1460 (kill gate), :2985 (flee sends the victim to stock_home). Captured state (seed 31, Mo at 8:45 pm day 2): all 5 transactional options (give coins, ask, lend, high-interest loan, pickpocket) targeted Tomas, the nearest; her brother Pip ('very fond') could not be chosen.
fundamentals.proposal: Options become verbs without targets ('Give someone 2 coins', 'Go talk with someone', 'Ask someone for food', 'Pick someone's pocket', 'Confront someone'). Each verb family gets a conditional who_<verb> choice over up to 12 known people (p_<id>: 'Pip, your brother; you are very fond of him; at home, 40 steps away'), answered in the same call and applied only if that verb is picked. This generalizes who_news from docs/society-spec.md section 6.2. The engine filters only for feasibility (alive, reachable, no violence against children). A victim who flees also answers a refuge choice: home, the police station, or the busy plaza. The added prompt size is small at about $0.0001 per call.
fundamentals.unlocks: providing for family, targeted kindness and charity, targeted revenge, favouritism, and manipulating a particular person

fundamentals.title: Perception ordered by salience and split into sections, before adding more villagers
fundamentals.problem: 'What you notice' is one flat list capped at 32 lines. Every visible villager comes first, then places, and the lines that matter most for the current call (debts, 'X just walked up to you') come last, so they are the first to be cut. Every visible villager is described in detail whether or not they matter to this person, so there is no attention. More villagers and children will break reply calls silently.
fundamentals.evidence: engine.ts:1002 (noticing.slice(0, 32)); engine.ts:906-914 (people first). Measured by adding cloned villagers into view: with 24 visible, the debt line and the 'just walked up to you' line were dropped; with 34 visible, the home-pantry line was dropped too. With today's 15 villagers: 25 lines. Random fake, seed 31, 3 days: median state 3,402 characters plus 4,292 characters of options, about 1,924 tokens per decide.
fundamentals.proposal: Split perception into sections, each with its own cap and ordering. situation: never truncated, specific to the call (who addressed you, what they want, the stakes, your debts to or from them). people: ranked by |liking| + highest belief importance + active emotion + a proximity term + whether they are addressing you, capped at 8, then 'and 14 others around the plaza'. places: only those relevant to current needs, the intention or beliefs. Option lists get the same relevance cap but always keep options involving the person addressing you and the current intention.
fundamentals.unlocks: more villagers, population growth and reproduction, and crowded events such as funerals, fights and markets, without reply calls losing their context

fundamentals.title: World time should wait for villagers' decisions instead of running on network time
fundamentals.problem: The live clock advances every 260 ms whether or not JEV has answered. A slow answer leaves the villager frozen 'thinking' for many ticks, and the answer is then applied to a world that has moved on, because perception was built when the request was sent. The lab instead waits for answers, landing each one a fixed number of ticks after its request (--think), so live and lab runs are systematically different minds. A persistent live world will also behave differently depending on network conditions.
fundamentals.evidence: components/sandbox/use-sandbox.ts:18 (BASE_TICK_MS=260), :266-275 (ticks advance without checking pending requests); scripts/lab.ts:86-91 (answers land 'think' ticks after the request). Real latency from the recorded lab runs: median 256 ms, p90 2,397 ms, max 6,758 ms. Derived: a p90 answer freezes a villager for about 9 ticks (45 in-game minutes) at 1x and about 36 ticks at 4x.
fundamentals.proposal: Use logical time in the live driver: the world advances tick N only when every request issued at or before N - think has been answered or has failed, exactly as the lab does, and the renderer smooths the motion. Combined with interrupt-driven reconsideration (the intentions item above), decisions then happen when events occur rather than at the pace of the network. This complements the persistence work already in flight rather than replacing it.
fundamentals.unlocks: live runs equal lab and replay runs, trustworthy experiments on the persistent world, and decision timing that reflects the character rather than the network

fundamentals.title: Make personality drift visible to JEV
fundamentals.problem: psycheLines names a Big Five trait only above 66 or below 34, foundations only above 70 or below 30, and values only by their top-3 order. Most drift is therefore invisible to JEV and then flips all at once; whether a change shows up depends on how close the villager started to a threshold. Children render almost nothing. The shadow line states 'you will not be caught' as if it were a fact about the world. Joining with 'and' makes lines hard to parse ('achievement and doing well and safety and stability').
fundamentals.evidence: psyche.ts:131 (thresholds), :160 (shadow wording), :124 (joining with 'and'). Measured by applying the same reflection outcome every night until any word changed: Hazel, Mo and Linnea change after 1 night for several outcomes; under more_ruthless, Odile, Sable, Lark, Kit and Tansy show no change after 30 nights, and under closer_to_family Ivy and Mo show none after 30. Kit (a child) renders 2 lines.
fundamentals.proposal: Add one line, 'How you have been changing', built from agent.drift: the last 1 or 2 reflection changes with their cause and when they started ('Lately you have grown more wary of people, since Pip lied to you on Tuesday'). Add graded wording for 55 to 65 and 35 to 45 ('somewhat outgoing'). Apply the spec's render-v2 fixes (semicolon joins, 'when you think you can get away with it'). Bump PSYCHE_RENDER_VERSION because this is an experimental change.
fundamentals.unlocks: traits that visibly evolve from behaviour, changing course after a formative event, and different psychologies producing different paths over time

summary: Fernhollow has coins, shops and payroll, but no economy in the game-theoretic sense. Money cannot change what a villager survives on, owns or builds, and the one exploit on offer (gouging) pays the gouger nothing, because shop tills belong to nobody. Coins are conserved but flow one way: county grant -> treasury -> wage earners -> tills -> delivery truck. Every till hit zero by day 2 to 4 under every policy I ran. That kills the farmer's only market, while food and idle money pile up in different houses. Food is not scarce: the free berry commons alone covers about 96% of the town's hunger, and total capacity is about 3x demand. So in real JEV runs the poorest villager never fished diligently, nobody collapsed, and about one work hour a day satisfies purpose. The repeated game has a short memory (memories last about 17 to 30 hours, and the favours ledger never reaches JEV), so cooperation and defection are effectively one-shot. Smallest fixes, in order: give each business an owner (till -> owner), make food a scarce, perishable flow, add person-to-person trade with JEV-chosen terms, then a per-pair ledger, property and capital, labor contracts, and fiscal decisions.

fundamentals.title: Businesses belong to nobody: the till is a one-way sink, so trade, gouging and self-employment pay nothing
fundamentals.problem: Shop.till is business money kept apart from the keeper's own purse, and no code path ever moves till coins into a purse. The till pays only the delivery truck, local producers and sales tax. Sable, Mo and Lark therefore have zero income by construction, yet their perception says 'You live on what you sell', and the gouging option promises 'you keep the difference'. The exploit is fake, so the price choice has no stakes and cooperative versus exploitative pricing is not a real dilemma. JEV clearly wants to gouge: it puts real probability on the high price.
fundamentals.evidence: lib/sim/types.ts:116 ('Business money, separate from the keeper's own purse'). Every till write (engine.ts:1801, 1817, 1833, 2385-2388, 2396-2397, found by grep) credits the truck, a producer or the treasury, never a keeper. False claims at engine.ts:924 and engine.ts:1169. Measured with a heuristic policy over 7 days: Sable ends at 274 coins whether the price is 3, 4 or 7, while the other villagers end at 947, 934 and 856 (gouging moves about 78 coins into a till that only pays the truck). Over 14 days Mo went 80 -> 56 and Lark 85 -> 47 while working. Real JEV (runs/fernhollow-founders-s600-20260923233212, replayed before the first desync at tick 233): Sable put p=0.09-0.20 on price_high and 0.00 on fair and cheap in all 7 decisions he made inside the store.
fundamentals.proposal: Add ownerId to Shop (sable, mo, lark) and treat the till as the owner's business account. Minimal version, a few lines in townDay: at the 6 pm close, profit above a 20-coin float moves to the owner's purse, with a memory line 'You took home N coins from the till'. Add own-store intents deposit_till and withdraw_till (the spec 2.3 verbs fetch_from_own_store and stock_own_store), offered only inside your own shop. Show the owner the till, today's revenue, cost of goods and margin. Fix the two false texts. Gouging then raises the owner's purse and customers' resentment, which is a live dilemma.
fundamentals.unlocks: buy/sell/exploit with real payoffs; market power; charity pricing that costs the giver; self-employed labor incentives; the spec's role-versus-person pricing experiment

fundamentals.title: No scarcity: a free commons covers about 96% of food demand and capacity is about 3x demand
fundamentals.problem: Coins are optional for survival, so nobody is forced into trade-offs. Working, charity, food theft and hoarding have almost no material consequence. Nothing spoils, so surpluses pile up forever. The option text also misstates physics: it says berries only take the edge off hunger, but a berry equals a cooked meal.
fundamentals.evidence: 6 bushes x 1 berry per 60 ticks (engine.ts:61) = 28.8 berries a day. One berry eaten on the spot gives 3 ticks x +12 = +36 hunger (engine.ts:2300), the same as cook_home at 6 x +6 (engine.ts:2306), against the text at engine.ts:1049. Town hunger drain is about 1080 a day (0.3 per tick awake, x0.35 asleep, persona multipliers), or 30 portions. Capacity is about 100 portions a day (berries 29 + farm 24 + fish 12 + truck 20 + diner 15). There is no spoilage code anywhere in lib/sim. In a 14-day heuristic run, home food rose 30 -> 283 portions (all in the Harrow and Reed houses) with 0 collapses. Real JEV: Hollis (2 coins) put 0.00 on work_diligent in all 12 pre-desync decisions where it was offered and fished only by coasting (twice); both Fernhollow runs had 0 collapses. Pip, the farmer, spent 24 of his 30 coins buying store groceries after stocking his own produce at home.
fundamentals.proposal: (a) Replace the integer carry, homeFood and stock with FoodStack {kind, n, madeTick}, using the spec 2.3 shelf lives (berries 2 days, fish 1, produce 3, groceries 5) and a spoiled counter. (b) Make berries a visible, depletable commons: regrow 1 per 240 ticks (about 7 a day, 25% of demand), with perception stating how many are left. That makes 'gather to carry' against 'leave some for others' a real dilemma. (c) Make the option text match the physics. (d) Add a calibration test with a needs-greedy policy: if everyone works, nobody spends more than 1 hour a day below hunger 15; if the producers shirk, someone does. Target supply at 1.1-1.3x demand.
fundamentals.unlocks: real trade-offs; providing for family; charity and food theft with consequences; the commons dilemma; famine interventions that bite

fundamentals.title: No trade between villagers, and every amount is fixed
fundamentals.problem: The Offer union has gifts, pleas, loans and pickpocketing, but no exchange. Producers can sell only to the store, which buys only while its till can pay. Once the till empties (day 2 to 4), the farmer and fisher have no market, and food and money sit in different houses with no way to meet. Every amount is hard-coded (gift 2 coins, loan 5 -> 6 or 5 -> 9, prices 3/4/7, pickpocket up to 3), so JEV cannot express how generous or how greedy someone is, or haggle.
fundamentals.evidence: types.ts Offer union. engine.ts:1147 (sell requires store.till >= buyPrice). Fixed amounts at engine.ts:1297, 1323, 1330, 1160-1180 and 78 (PICKPOCKET_MAX). In the 14-day heuristic run, 283 portions sat in 2 houses while Bram, Tomas and Mo spent 430-595 ticks below hunger 25 walking to the woods, and 1646 private coins sat idle. Decide calls carry a median of 29 options (p95 34, max 37) against the wire cap of 64 (schema.ts:69), so terms cannot be added as extra options.
fundamentals.proposal: Add Offer {kind:'trade', give:{food?|coins?|assetId?}, get:{...}}. Add the options 'Offer to sell food to X' and 'Offer to buy food from X' for the 1 to 3 nearest people (the existing TALK_OPTIONS). Terms go in a side question inside the same decide call, not in the option list: terms_<optionId> is a choice over about 6 honestly labelled price tiers ('1 coin a portion, below what the store pays' up to '8 coins, twice the store price'). It is asked only for the trade options present and used only if that option wins. The responder chooses accept, counter (one tier their way, which triggers one more respond from the asker) or refuse. The same tier mechanism sets gift and loan amounts. This is an ultimatum and bargaining game that can be measured per psyche.
fundamentals.unlocks: buying and selling between people; manipulation (overcharging the desperate); kindness (selling below cost); haggling; measurable generosity; self-organizing trade networks

fundamentals.title: Wealth buys nothing that lasts: no property, tools or capital to build, own, steal or destroy
fundamentals.problem: Coins can be spent only on three consumables, or given away and lent. So the 'grow rich' goal means nothing, inequality has no effect on anyone's options, there is no investment-versus-consumption trade-off, and apart from the footbridge there is nothing to build, rearrange or destroy. Claudio's 'destroy someone's house and they are pissed' has no object to act on.
fundamentals.evidence: The only villager coin sinks are at engine.ts:1117-1153 (dine, bar, buy). Agent holds only coins and carry (types.ts Agent). The wealth goal exists in lib/jev/schema.ts GOALS. In the 14-day heuristic run, Sable held 274-280 coins with nothing to buy, Odile went 60 -> 215 and Hazel 150 -> 210. In real JEV, Sable spent 6 of 280 coins, on one meal. The spec covers home deeds (spec 2.5) but no capital goods.
fundamentals.proposal: Add Asset {id, kind: 'tool'|'cart'|'boat'|'stall'|'field_plot'|'house_upgrade'|'fence', ownerId, pos?, condition 0-100, value, builtBy[]} and World.assets. Effects: a rod multiplies fish x1.5, a plough multiplies produce x1.5, a cart raises carry from 6 to 12, and a house upgrade adds respect and a visible sprite. Wren builds assets from wood (east woods, 1 an hour; spec Slice B) plus hours, and they change hands through the trade offer. New verbs: damage and destroy (a crime against the owner, feeding wrongedBy and a new life event 'property_destroyed'), repair, and inheritance by the household. First slice: Wren's workshop sells a rod and a plough.
fundamentals.unlocks: building things; destroying someone's property with lasting grievance; investment versus consumption; inheritance; envy and inequality that matter; the carpenter as a real business

fundamentals.title: The repeated game has a short memory and no reputation
fundamentals.problem: Villagers rarely act on a partner's track record because the prompt rarely carries it. Memory holds 14 entries and shows 7. The favours ledger is written but never shown. A lender sees no credit history. Third parties learn about a default or a theft only by seeing it or reading the Crier. The shadow of the future is weak, so cooperation-versus-defection choices behave like one-shot games and tit-for-tat cannot emerge.
fundamentals.evidence: engine.ts:65-66 (MEMORY_KEEP 14, MEMORY_IN_PROMPT 7). Median memory lifetime before eviction is 17.3 h under the fake JEV (p90 23.4 h) and 29.5 h under the heuristic (p90 42.8 h). fundamentals.title: Production chains are cut and supply is a fixed standing order
fundamentals.problem: The diner and inn buy nothing locally, and meals come only from the truck. The store orders 20 units a day whatever is already on the shelf, and nobody decides inventory. So there is no farm -> store/diner -> customer chain, local producers never compete with imports, and tills bleed to zero regardless of behaviour. The cook cannot use her own kitchen.
fundamentals.evidence: buyPrice 0 for the diner and inn (engine.ts:238-239). Fixed order at engine.ts:85 and 2385-2388. Heuristic run: the store had 51 units on day 1 and the truck still took 60 coins, draining the till 80 -> 2. Shelf stock then sat at 52-68 for 12 days. Real JEV replay: the store till fell 80 -> 42 in one day, with 6 units sold. Stale-meal bug: deliver() returns before resetting meals when the till cannot pay (engine.ts:2386), so a broke diner's meals never perish (stock 6 with a till of 1 for 10 days). Real JEV at 8:45 pm on day 1: Mo, hunger 21, with 10 unsold meals and 60 coins in her diner's till and 80 in her purse, asked two neighbours for food, because she has no verb to eat from her own kitchen.
fundamentals.proposal: Give the diner a kitchen with ingredient stock: a meal = 1 ingredient + 6 ticks of the cook's time. When Pip or Hollis offer produce, Mo gets an accept_sale respond (take_all, take_some, refuse; already designed in spec 2.3). The store buys produce and fish at a posted buy price. The truck becomes an order the owner picks at shift start (0, 5, 10 or 20 units at 3 coins). Local produce at 2 undercuts imports at 3, so the local chain wins only while producers actually work.
fundamentals.unlocks: a real production economy; interdependence (the cook needs the farmer); boycotts and strikes; shortages with a local cause

fundamentals.title: Labor has no material stakes and jobs are permanent
fundamentals.problem: About one diligent hour a day refills purpose, pay buys nothing anyone needs, and the self-employed earn nothing at all. Nobody can be hired, dismissed or employ someone else. Observed attendance (36-40%) therefore reflects persona wording, not incentives, and there is no principal-agent game.
fundamentals.evidence: Purpose drains 0.1 per tick x rate (engine.ts:55; psyche.ts:183) = 16.5-37.3 a day. Diligent work adds 2.5 per tick for 12 ticks = +30 an hour (engine.ts:2325). So 0.55-1.24 hours a day refills purpose for every villager, against posted shifts of 6-13 hours (jobs.ts). Shirk test over 10 days: Sable ends at 280 shirking against 274-280 working, and Mo at 80 against 56-80, so working never raised their money. Salaried shirkers lost 27-117 coins that buy nothing they need. Real JEV attendance was 0.36 and 0.40. Persona.job is fixed data.
fundamentals.proposal: Add Employment {employer: 'town'|agentId, workerId, wage, hoursDue, warnings}. The mayor gets a weekly review duty question per town employee (keep, warn, dock pay, dismiss; spec M6, planned for Slice B), vacancies are posted on the notice board, and anyone can pick an 'apply' option. Private hiring via Offer {kind:'hire', wage tier, hours}: Pip can hire Hollis for field work, and Sable can hire a helper to keep the store open. Taper the purpose gain after 2 hours (x0.5), so duty and money, not purpose, carry a full shift.
fundamentals.unlocks: the principal-agent game; exploitation (low wages); kindness (generous wages); unemployment; real jobs; self-organized labor

fundamentals.title: Money supply is an open pipe with no fiscal decisions, and a rich villager breaks the wire
fundamentals.problem: 120 coins enter every day, and the only exit (deliveries) stops once the tills are empty, so money grows without bound. The treasury accumulates and nobody decides anything about it. In a persistent world, the first villager to hold more than 500 coins can no longer answer any offer, because the request fails validation.
fundamentals.evidence: engine.ts:83 and 2383-2389. In the 14-day heuristic run, coins_out stayed flat at 118 from day 2 while coins_in reached 1680; the treasury went 600 -> 1749 and private coins 1180 -> 1646. Real JEV day 1: treasury 600 -> 649 and 600 -> 655 (payroll 73 against a 120 grant). The mayor's work only adds respect (finishWork). schema.ts:93 caps can.coins at 500; I verified that a respond wire with can.coins=501 fails jevRequestSchema, which both app/api/jev/route.ts:8 and runJev in lib/jev/call.ts enforce. At 40 coins a day, the doctor reaches 500 in about 2 weeks of full attendance.
fundamentals.proposal: Now: clamp can.coins and can.food in startAsking (they only bound the replies) or raise the cap, and add money-stock metrics (private coins, tills, treasury). Then give the mayor a weekly budget duty: a choice of tax tier (0/5/10/20%) and a choice of spending (project materials, relief to the poorest, a bonus for workers, or save), plus a private take_from_treasury option recorded in a readable ledger (designed in spec M6). Add real sinks: imported materials for assets, and clinic supplies. Tune the grant so the money stock stays about flat under the needs-greedy policy.
fundamentals.unlocks: institutions; a public-goods game; embezzlement; tax politics; a persistent world that stays stable

fundamentals.title: Economic decisions are buried in the action list with fixed tiers, and shops close whenever the keeper is deciding
fundamentals.problem: Setting a price competes with 'work this hour' inside one choice, so min-p sampling never lets a price change through, even when JEV clearly leans toward gouging. Only the store has prices at all; diner and inn prices are hard-coded. And shopOpen requires the keeper to be mid-work, so a keeper standing inside and deciding counts as closed.
fundamentals.evidence: Price options appear only while Sable decides inside the store (engine.ts:1157-1180). MIN_P is 0.25 of the favourite (engine.ts pickFrom, around line 2610). Real JEV: price_high at 0.09-0.20 against work_diligent at 0.41-0.94, so it was never sampled, and the price stayed 4 all day in both Fernhollow runs. Diner and inn prices are fixed at engine.ts:238-239. The open check (engine.ts:337-348) requires status acting:work. Traced: Lark reached the general store while Sable was idle inside it and was turned away. found_closed was 262-302 per 14 days in heuristic runs, and 2 and 10 in the two real 1-day runs.
fundamentals.proposal: At a role holder's first shift decision each day, add duty side questions to the same decide call: price_<good> (a choice over honestly labelled markup tiers, from the spec 2.3 table), order_<good> and buy_price_<good>. They go in decideQuestions in lib/jev/prompt.ts alongside mood and motive and are applied directly, with no extra call (the spec's C3 set_prices, 'up to 3 price questions in one call'). Count a keeper as serving whenever they are inside their shop during their shift, whatever their status.
fundamentals.unlocks: measuring market power per psyche (role versus person); price dynamics; gouging in shortages; economic decisions that are easy to read in the UI
