lens: Longevity of a persistent world, and scientific validity of "authentic decisions"
summary: The engine is deterministic, but only as long as its own code never changes. A live world that runs for weeks across deploys needs versioned snapshots as its source of truth, and today there are none. None of the 13 recorded runs replays on HEAD. Four of them cannot be replayed on any commit because they were recorded on uncommitted code. The desync counter reports 0 while it applies 93 answers to the wrong villagers. Time compression makes every long-run problem arrive fast: at 1x the world runs 48 in-game days per real hour. In that time trait drift hits its hard cap, the population can only shrink (no births, no aging, no one takes over a dead person's job), and money grows by exactly the county grant whatever anyone does. On validity: position and content are fully confounded (eat is first in 93% of menus and rest is last in 100%). The trajectory is chaotic because of one shared RNG stream: one answer delayed by one tick changes all 15 villagers within 13 in-game hours. Min-p 0.25 quietly halves crime and removes almost all gifts and loans. Some option text promises consequences the engine does not implement. The JEV judge gives the same verdict under every condition. So nothing in the repo can yet tell JEV's psychology apart from our menu design, and the fixes below are what make "authentic decisions" a claim you can defend.

fundamentals.title: Versioned snapshot chain as the source of truth, with integrity-checked, epoch-scoped event logs
fundamentals.problem: Replaying from seed plus events only works on the exact code that recorded it, and nothing records which code that was. RECORD_VERSION stayed 1 across four different engines. RunEvent matches answers to requests only by a global sequence number, so replaying on the wrong code puts answers on the wrong villagers and still reports 0 desyncs. The in-flight checkpoint has three gaps: it is one blob that each save overwrites (no history), it carries no engine or prompt version, and it keeps no events. hydrateWorld only fills in missing keys, so code changes to the map or personas (new buildings, new people, edited personas) never reach a saved world, and new fields arrive with their genesis values. The evidence behind decisions also disappears: STATES_KEPT keeps only 3 state texts per villager.
fundamentals.evidence: Measured: replaying all 13 runs/*.json.gz on HEAD gives desyncs up to 638/653 and wrong populations (15 vs 10 or 4). Replaying each run on its own commit (scratch git archive): 6 replay cleanly, psyche-founders-s200 (292/356), economy-v1 (524/622) and both fernhollow runs (88/387, 48/334) desync on every commit. Silent corruption: scarcity-baseline-s100 on HEAD reports desyncs 0 but applies 93 of 105 decide answers to a different 15-person town and logs 43 'Unusable JEV answer ... unknown option talk_juniper'. lib/sim/session.ts:13 RECORD_VERSION = 1, lines 16-27 (RunEvent has no agentId/kind/stateHash). lib/sim/checkpoint.ts:9 CHECKPOINT_VERSION = 1, :17 STATES_KEPT = 3, :79 hydrateWorld (additive fill only). lib/live/store.ts writes one live/<id>.json.gz. Snapshot 970 KB JSON (143 KB gzip), 843 KB of it decisions[].state. Event log about 197 KB per in-game day raw.
fundamentals.proposal: (1) lib/sim/version.ts: ENGINE_VERSION (VERCEL_GIT_COMMIT_SHA, or a build-time content hash of lib/sim/** and lib/jev/** in dev); PROMPT_HASH = FNV-1a of buildState and decideQuestions rendered on a fixed fixture perception, so any wording change changes the hash; PSYCHE_RENDER_VERSION. Stamp all three on Checkpoint, RunRecord and every DecisionRecord. (2) Immutable history: live/<id>/cp/<day>.json.gz once per in-game day plus a head pointer, instead of overwriting a single blob. (3) Epoch segments: {fromCheckpointKey, engineVersion, events[]} appended as JSONL chunks. A deploy that changes ENGINE_VERSION closes the segment and writes a boundary checkpoint. ReplayCursor refuses a segment whose engineVersion is not the running code. (4) RunEvent gains agentId, kind and stateHash; any mismatch on apply counts as a desync and stops the replay. (5) Explicit MIGRATIONS: Record<number, (cp) => cp>, plus a fixture test that loads a stored v(n-1) checkpoint and runs invariants. Map and persona changes become migrations, not silent code edits. (6) Content-addressed evidence: store state text once as states/<sha256>.txt in Blob and keep only the hash in the DecisionRecord, so evidence never has to be dropped to keep checkpoints small.
fundamentals.unlocks: A fully stateful world that survives reloads and deploys for weeks; being able to audit why something happened on day 40; defensible replays

fundamentals.title: Make world time independent of network latency: per-agent RNG streams and a fixed think time
fundamentals.problem: Every random draw in the world (wander target, min-p roll, chat and press Bernoulli draws) shares one mulberry32 state on world.rng. Any perturbation therefore spreads chaotically through everyone. In live mode an answer is applied whenever it happens to arrive, so network latency, tab throttling and pause/resume all change history. The lab applies answers after exactly 1 tick, so lab and live are different experimental conditions. Paired A/B runs (same seed, one fact changed) cannot be interpreted.
fundamentals.evidence: Measured butterfly test (scratch zz/butterfly.ts, same seed, answers keyed per agent and call so the policy is identical): delaying ONE answer by one tick made 281 of 288 ticks differ, up to 15/15 agents (8/15 by hour 4), with 65 of 90 counters different after one day. The same test on a scratch copy with keyed per-agent RNG (7-line patch of the 4 nextRandom sites at engine.ts:1495, 2624, 3019, 3068): 1 tick differs, 1 agent, 0 counters. Real JEV latency across 4,048 recorded answers: p50 290 ms, p90 2,426 ms, p99 6,656 ms. At BASE_TICK_MS 260 (use-sandbox.ts:18) that is 9 ticks stale at p90 at 1x and 37 ticks at 4x, while the lab uses think=1 (scripts/lab.ts).
fundamentals.proposal: Replace world.rng with rand(world, agentId, stream) = hash32(seed, agentId, stream, agent.rngCounters[stream]++). The counters live on Agent, so they are saved in the snapshot. Use streams 'wander', 'choice:<questionId>', 'engage', 'press' and 'shuffle', plus a 'physics' stream per entity for world events. Give every SimRequest dueTick = tick + THINK_TICKS (recorded in WorldConfig, e.g. 3). The driver applies answers exactly at dueTick in request-id order, and holds the world clock if a due answer has not arrived (a stall, not a divergence). History then depends only on (snapshot, answers), so pause, resume, reload and speed changes are invisible and live equals lab.
fundamentals.unlocks: Pause when no browser is open and resume later with the same history; A/B experiments and ablations you can interpret; live and lab results being comparable

fundamentals.title: Decision provenance plus a counterfactual re-ask harness (shuffle, reword, psyche swap, one-fact change)
fundamentals.problem: Options are always shown in authored order: body first, then work, commons, people, justice, violence, leisure, and rest last. Position and content are therefore fully confounded: any primacy bias JEV has shows up as 'villagers eat sensibly'. Nothing is logged that would let anyone separate the psychology effect from the effects of wording, order or option count. There is no shown order, no prompt version, no eligible set and no stale-ticks record. PSYCHE_RENDER_VERSION is declared and never recorded. The spec (docs/society-spec.md 1793, 2446) plans a seeded shuffle and version logging, but the live code implements none of it.
fundamentals.evidence: Real JEV data (1,413 decisions from 5 runs replayed on their own commits, scratch longev/jev_dist.ts and analyze.ts): position 0 was 'eat' in 1,317/1,413 (93%), the last position was 'rest' in 1,413/1,413. The first 40% of positions hold 66.1% of JEV's probability mass while making up 42.3% of options. p_top falls from 0.54 on 9-15 option menus to 0.44 on 24-28 option menus (observational). The current engine has the same order: eat at relative position 0.02, rest at 1.00 (zz/wording.ts). grep: PSYCHE_RENDER_VERSION appears only at lib/sim/psyche.ts:9. Cost per call $0.000085 (mean over recorded answers).
fundamentals.proposal: (1) Seeded shuffle of options per call from rand(agent,'shuffle'). Log shownOrder, and keep a fixed order only as an ablation arm. (2) A DecisionLog row per call: {decisionId, tick, agentId, kind, engineVersion, promptHash, stateHash, shownOrder, full probability vector, eligible ids, prunedMass, roll, picked, staleTicks, stillValidAtApply}, written to the segment log. (3) scripts/probe-jev.ts: sample N recorded decisions, rebuild the exact state from the content-addressed store, apply one named perturbation (shuffle, reverse, neutral_details, no_psyche, swap_psyche:<otherId>, drop_option:<verb>, fact:hunger+30, affinity_flip:<id>, action_only with no motive/mood questions), re-ask JEV, and report mean |Δp| and argmax flip rate with bootstrap CIs. (4) A pre-registered claim rule: call behaviour 'psychology-driven' only if the psyche-swap effect is at least 3x the shuffle and neutral-wording effects. 1,000 probes cost about $0.09.
fundamentals.unlocks: Defensible claims that decisions are authentic; different drivers for different psychologies, measured rather than assumed; checking that trait evolution actually changes decisions

fundamentals.title: Baseline policies as control worlds, and a judge calibrated against them
fundamentals.problem: The repo never compares JEV with a random, greedy or position-biased policy, so there is no measure of how much of the society comes from the menu and the physics rather than from JEV. The 'interestingness' judge gets an OWNER_BRIEF listing the exact features to look for (murder, exploiting, charity ...) and a digest made of feature counters. Its 'missing' answer can only name one of our own roadmap keys. It is never shown a control.
fundamentals.evidence: Expected antisocial picks per 1,000 real decisions (pickpocket, lie, usury, take): uniform random 87.6, JEV with min-p 4.9, JEV argmax 2.8. Explore: uniform 223 vs JEV 48 (zz/policies.ts). So JEV clearly is not random, but nothing in the repo computes this. After one day, the random-policy (tests/fake-jev) digest already contains attacks, lies, usurious loans and murders: 16 of its 58 summary lines are crime or violence (zz/digest_probe.ts). Over 30 days that random policy took the town from 15 to 3 alive with 77 crimes (seed 31). Nine judged runs in the session lab logs, across 6 different conditions (psyche, economy, drift engine, drift jev, town, justice), got identical labels 9/9 ('villagers very distinct', 'a real community', best part 'psychology'), interest between 1.44 and 2.02 out of 4, and 'missing' was always a roadmap key (conflict_and_justice 5/9). prompt.ts:255 OWNER_BRIEF, :301 missing criteria = ASSESS_ROADMAP.
fundamentals.proposal: lib/sim/policies.ts exports answer functions with the same shape as fakeAnswer: uniform, needs_greedy (lowest need first, never antisocial), first_option, jev_argmax. WorldConfig.policy selects one, and Session and lab run it through the same pipeline (lab --policy). Every reported metric becomes 'JEV minus control' over at least 5 seeds. Judge: make it pairwise (a JEV run against a control digest, random order, blinded titles), remove the feature checklist from OWNER_BRIEF, and add a discrimination question ('which run was produced by random choices?'). Trust it only once it prefers JEV runs over uniform-policy runs at least 80% of the time. Use its 'missing' output as advice only, never as roadmap evidence.
fundamentals.unlocks: A genuinely interesting social experiment (measured against chance); honest live metrics; roadmap choices that do not rest on a judge that agrees with everything

fundamentals.title: Make the sampling rule a declared, logged experimental parameter
fundamentals.problem: MIN_P = 0.25 is a hidden constant that changes the moral makeup of the society, and question types use different rules: min-p for decide and for the reflection change, goal, gratitude and grudge answers; raw Bernoulli(p) for chat engage and press-on; argmax for the reflection 'keep' answer. JEV is a calibrated evaluator, so its distribution is its belief, and min-p systematically cuts off the rare-but-plausible tail on both the kind and the cruel side.
fundamentals.evidence: From 1,413 real decisions: min-p removes on average 20.0% of JEV's mass (p90 35%, max 58%). The median decision has 3 eligible options, and 24% of decisions have just 1 (effectively argmax). Expected per 1,000 decisions, with full calibrated sampling vs min-p 0.25 vs argmax: gifts plus loans 3.4 / 0.1 / 0; antisocial 10.3 / 4.9 / 2.8; P(pick differs from argmax) 0.51 vs 0.38. Code: engine.ts:2616 MIN_P, 2624 roll; 3019 press and 3068 engage use nextRandom < p; reflection keep uses keep.choice (argmax) while change and goal use pickFrom.
fundamentals.proposal: WorldConfig.sampling = {rule: 'full' | 'minp' | 'argmax', minP}, recorded in the checkpoint and the run. One sample(world, agentId, questionId, probs) function for every choice, boolean and score-level question. Log the eligible set and pruned mass per decision (see provenance). Use 'full' as the default arm for authenticity claims and 'minp 0.25' as a named ablation, and report crime, kindness and economy metrics for each arm.
fundamentals.unlocks: Being kind or charitable, crime, exploitation and manipulation arising at JEV's own rates instead of at a rate fixed by one constant

fundamentals.title: Menus with mechanics-backed consequences, a neutral-wording arm, and verb/target factoring
fundamentals.problem: The menu is the policy's prior, and at present it is a moral text. Every antisocial verb carries a warning and no prosocial verb does. Some warnings describe consequences that do not exist. The engine picks victims and beneficiaries, not JEV. Option count inflates some categories. Several reply questions change nothing but the wording of a memory, so their outcome is fixed in advance and they tell us nothing about authenticity.
fundamentals.evidence: Wording audit of the current engine (zz/wording.ts): take, lie, usury, pickpocket, shove, attack and kill all carry warning clauses; the give_coins detail is 11 words and carries none. engine.ts:1169 price_high says 'People who notice may resent it', but set_price (around 1962-1972) only sets shop.price and logs, with no affinity or perception effect. engine.ts:1464 kill says 'the town may never forgive you', but die() (1554-1590) only moves affinity for witnesses who were already fond of the victim (-0.6). Explore takes 7 options per menu (5,936 explore options across 848 menus). Targets are chosen by the engine: gift, ask, lie, lend, usury and pickpocket only toward the nearest person (1281); violence only toward the lowest-affinity adult within 8 steps (1441); kill only with a grudge or affinity <= -0.4. Clone-and-diff test (zz/decorative.ts, 4 seeds): for attack replies, plead, call_help and take_it gave identical world states in 29 of 46 cases; warn accept and argue were identical; arrest go_quietly and protest differ only in memory text (2907-2928).
fundamentals.proposal: OptionSpec gains effects: EffectId[], and the detail text is rendered only from an EFFECTS table ('anyone within 6 steps will see', 'costs 5 coins', 'the shopkeeper's customers see the new price'). tests/consequences.test.ts applies each effect-bearing option or reply to a cloned world and asserts the state change the wording claims. A reply whose options produce identical states fails the test. Add an ablation wording: 'authored' | 'neutral' (mechanical facts only). Factor social verbs: first pick a verb, then run a second JEV choice 'who' over the people in sight (at most 255 options, which fits JEV), or list verb x target when it fits. Collapse explore_* into one option followed by a 'where' choice. Give arrest a resist/flee reply with real consequences, and give call_help a real mechanic (nearby people get a respond call).
fundamentals.unlocks: Choosing whom to help, rob or hurt, and why (psychology driving the choice); 'destroy someone's house and they get angry' being grounded in state; honest option text

fundamentals.title: Long-run stationarity: demography, role seats, mean-reverting drift and money sinks
fundamentals.problem: At 48 in-game days per real hour, a world that runs for weeks lives through thousands of in-game days, and every stock variable heads to an absorbing boundary. Population: death comes only from violence, and there are no births, no arrivals and no aging. Roles: jobs are fixed on the persona and shops have a fixed keeperId, so a dead shopkeeper or officer means that institution is gone for good. Cases whose suspect is dead stay open. Money: the county grant arrives no matter what anyone does, and nothing drains money in proportion to how much exists. Personality: drift has a hard ±25 wall and no pull back toward the original, so the cap, not experience, ends up defining who people are. Collapse never kills, so starvation becomes a repeating nap.
fundamentals.evidence: Measured, 30-day runs (zz/longrun.ts). Random policy: 15 to 3 alive by day 21 (seed 31; seed 32: 3 by day 30), 10 open cases frozen from day 15. Needs-greedy benign policy: 131 collapses and 0 deaths. Money supply followed the same path under both policies, 1,843 to 5,279 and 5,285 (+120 per day, the grant), with shop tills stuck at 2 coins from day 10 so deliveries stopped. Prices are constants inside option ids (4/7/3, engine.ts:1160-1177). Drift, bootstrapped from 27 real JEV reflections through lib/sim/drift.ts (zz/driftsim.ts): first path hits the ±25 cap on day 14 (about 17 real minutes at 1x); 29 paths by day 100; 74 by day 300; 8 of 15 villagers' trust pinned at the cap by day 100. engine.ts:197 keeperId fixed; die() is called only from the two violence paths (around 2981 and 3046); persona.age is only ever rendered as text; drift.ts:22-24 DAILY_CAP 3 and LIFETIME_CAP 25.
fundamentals.proposal: (a) Seats: world.seats: Record<JobId, {holderId|null, since}>. shopOpen and officerOf look up the seat holder. A vacancy (death, jail, quitting) triggers a JEV 'apply' boolean for eligible adults and a mayor 'appoint' choice. (b) Demography: age advances at lifePace years per in-game day; coming of age at 16; a natural-death hazard; births from partnered households (two JEV consent booleans); an 'arrival' event when population falls below a floor, using a persona generator. (c) Drift: nightly psyche += 0.02 x (birth - psyche), and scale each delta by (1 - |deviation|/40) instead of a hard wall, so the long-run personality reflects how often things happen. (d) Money: the treasury funds public works and wages by rule, there is a stock-proportional sink (spoilage or upkeep), and prices are relative levels (cost plus a margin chosen by JEV) rather than constants. (e) Weekly stationarity metrics (alive, births minus deaths, coins per capita, share of traits at the cap, vacant seats) with a trend alarm.
fundamentals.unlocks: Reproduction, more actors, groups forming over generations, a real economy, traits that keep changing, and a world that is never reset

fundamentals.title: Liveness invariants and bounded state for unattended runs
fundamentals.problem: There is no fallback brain, so any structural failure freezes a villager for good. The decide schema allows at most 64 options while menus keep growing with each feature. A rejected request backs off and rebuilds the same menu indefinitely. The deciding, asking and considering statuses have no timeout. Unbounded arrays (crimes, debts, cases, agent.knows) are scanned during every decision.
fundamentals.evidence: lib/jev/schema.ts:69 options .max(64). Current engine menus (zz/longrun.ts): p50 27-28, p99 41, max 52 (the officer Odile, random policy, seed 31), up from max 28 on the older engines. A request over 64 options is rejected by /api/jev, failRequest backs off ERROR_BACKOFF_TICKS 12, and step() rebuilds the same menu. engine.ts:2513 'case deciding: break' with no timeout. In 30 random-policy days: 77 crimes, 46 debts, 246 knows entries, 15 cases (10 stuck open). The officer's open_ loop at engine.ts:1387 does world.crimes.find inside agent.knows, which is O(knows x crimes). Per-tick cost is not a problem yet (0.16-0.28 ms per tick, 46-83 ms per in-game day).
fundamentals.proposal: lib/sim/invariants.ts checkWorld(world) runs every in-game hour in lab and tests and before every checkpoint write. It checks: menu length within the cap (truncate by salience and log 'truncated', or raise the cap toward JEV's 255 together with the factoring in the menu fundamental); no agent waiting more than MAX_WAIT ticks (auto-fail and log); every referenced agent id alive or its record resolved (close cases whose suspect or victim has died); coins and food conserved; exactly one status per agent. Move resolved debts, cases, crimes and lies older than 7 in-game days out of the snapshot into the history segment. Store crimes in a Record keyed by id.
fundamentals.unlocks: A world that runs unattended for days; performance audits that stay flat over long runs

lens: performance and scalability (measured with the fake JEV, plus the 13 recorded real-JEV runs in runs/)
summary:
Engine CPU is not the problem. step() takes 0.15-0.7 ms per tick at 15 villagers and 1.4-2.8 ms at 100, against a tick budget of 65-260 ms. perceive() and buildOptions() stay flat at about 0.1-0.2 ms per call over 30 days. The real limits sit elsewhere, and all four block what Claudio wants.
(1) The JEV call. A decide sends about 8.8K chars (about 2.2K tokens), and 52% of that is the option list. Real JEV leaves only 2.67 of 25 options eligible under min-p. Decide calls cost twice as much as respond calls, and their p90 latency is 5x higher (2.49 s vs 0.48 s).
(2) Wall-clock coupling. The live loop never waits for JEV, so the same seed runs a different society at each speed: villagers are frozen 15%, 21% and 33% of the time at 1x, 2x and 4x.
(3) What gets persisted. The shipped checkpoint is 183 KB gzipped every 8 s, 73% of it decision traces. The replay log is never persisted, and genesis replay already desyncs on recorded real runs.
(4) Perception built for 15 people. Villager lines come first in `noticing` and the list is cut at 32, so at 60 villagers 38% of decides lose the villager's own coins line, and 70% at 100.
Clock check: 5 minutes per tick means 288 ticks per day, not 144. `KEYFRAME_EVERY=144` is half a day.
Note: the persistence commit 2db20e2 landed while I was auditing, and I re-measured on it. It already removed the 600-call cap and the per-tick React re-render (renders are now held to at most 8.3 per second).

fundamentals.title: Perception budget that survives more actors: own facts first, salience-ranked people, an aggregate line
fundamentals.problem: perceive() pushes one line per visible villager first (engine.ts:908-915). Only after that come the villager's own money, job, shops, pantry and debts. Then it cuts at 32 lines (engine.ts:1002, schema.ts:56 max 32). As the population grows, crowds push the villager's own situation out of what JEV reads. Their choices then stop reflecting their own circumstances, which undermines authentic decisions.
fundamentals.evidence:
crowding.ts (clones placed at the founders' homes), percentage of decide requests:
- 15 agents: 0% at the cap.
- 30 agents: 10.5% at the cap.
- 60 agents: 65.8% at the cap; own coins line dropped 38.2%, job line 31.5%, chapel pantry line 29.2%.
- 100 agents: 79.7% at the cap; coins dropped 69.8%, job 59.2%, pantry 44.5%.
State text at 100 agents stays about 4.0K chars only because of this truncation.
fundamentals.proposal:
Build `noticing` from fixed-budget sections:
- Self facts (coins and carry, job and shift, home pantry, own debts, grief, jail) always come first and are never cut.
- Places, then public goods.
- People: the top K=8 by a salience score (same building > adjacent > currently interacting with me > |affinity| >= 0.35 or a grudge or gratitude > distance), followed by one aggregate line such as "23 others are around the plaza, mostly chatting; 4 are at the diner." This line is computed by grouping visible agents by `describeLocation` and status kind.

Implementation: in perceive(), build `people: {salience, line}[]`, sort, slice(0, 8), then add the aggregate line. Keep the zod max. This is pure and deterministic, and costs O(n log n) per call.
fundamentals.unlocks: More actors and reproduction, groups forming (the aggregate line is the natural place for crowds and factions), and decisions that stay grounded in the villager's own situation at scale

fundamentals.title: Factorize the decide call: verbs once, then whom and where as separate choice questions in the same evaluate call
fundamentals.problem: Every person-directed act is a cross-product of verb and target, and every place is its own long option. The list is expensive, mostly dead weight, and restricted by design: TALK_OPTIONS=3 nearest people (engine.ts:69,1260), and gifts, loans and pickpocketing only toward the single nearest person (engine.ts:1281). A villager cannot be kind to, or kill, someone who is not nearest. Adding people or verbs grows the list multiplicatively toward the 64-option zod cap.
fundamentals.evidence:
From validate.ts, factorize.ts and token-anatomy.ts over the fake runs:
- Decide input: state 3,483 chars + action criteria 4,537 + instructions 276 + motive 435 + mood 68, so criteria are 52% of the input.
- Person-targeted options are 38.1% of criteria (11.4 options over 3.63 distinct targets).
- The 7 explore_* options are 26.8% of criteria.
- Police officer peaked at 52 options, and 60 at 100 agents (cap 64).

From the real Fernhollow runs (558 decides):
- 25.2 options offered, only 2.67 eligible under min-p 0.25, 10.07 above 1%.
- Explore was picked 1.8% of the time.

From lat-by-size.ts over the real runs:
- Decide cost rises with option count: $0.000082 (<15), $0.000093 (15-21), $0.000109 (22-27), $0.000121 (28+).
- Respond (about 470 chars of questions): $0.000051, p90 481 ms. Decide: $0.000103, p90 2,486 ms, on a similar state size. This is a correlation, not proven causation.
fundamentals.proposal:
In decideQuestions:
- `action`: one criterion per verb ("chat with someone", "give food to someone", "pick someone's pocket", "attack someone", "explore somewhere", plus untargeted acts). Keep world-fixed joint options as is (repay_<debt>, report_<crime>, arrest_<case>).
- `whom`: a choice over visible, approachable villagers, up to 255, each labelled with name, distance and one-line status. Read it only when the chosen verb is targeted.
- `where`: the POI list with short labels.
- Ask `motive` on a deterministic 1-in-4 sample, since it is measurement-only.
- Move repeated boilerplate (explore and chat details) into the state once.

Engine side: OptionSpec gains `target: "person" | "place" | null`, and applyDecision resolves the target from the `whom` or `where` answer via pickFrom.

Caveat: independent questions lose the joint verb-by-target distribution. For violent verbs, confirm with the existing respond-sized `press` step. My estimate is -28% criteria chars at today's 3.6 targets. The larger gain is that cost now grows linearly, not multiplicatively, as targets are added.
fundamentals.unlocks: Kill, harm or be kind to anyone, not just the nearest person; more actors without hitting the option cap; lower cost per call and plausibly a shorter latency tail

fundamentals.title: Deterministic think time in game ticks, hedged calls and burst smoothing, so dynamics do not depend on speed or network
fundamentals.problem: The live clock never waits for JEV (use-sandbox.ts:283-290). An answer lands whenever the network delivers it, while lab lands it `think` ticks later (lab.ts:87-91). The same seed is a different society at 1x, 2x and 4x, and different again from lab. Results are neither comparable nor reproducible across sessions. Wake-up bursts send up to N simultaneous calls, which slows them all.
fundamentals.evidence:
latency-sim.ts replays the real latency distribution (2,592 answers: p50 282 ms, p90 2,454 ms, p99 6,687 ms):
- Villagers are frozen waiting on JEV 0% (lab), 15.3% (1x), 21.1% (2x), 33.0% (4x) of alive time.
- Decisions per day: 203, 171, 136, 113.

lat-by-size.ts: same-tick bursts of 9+ calls ran at p50 897 ms, vs 289 ms solo.

bench: requests per tick max = N at every scale (15/30/60/100).

barrier-sim.ts, strict lockstep (answer applied at issue+T, clock stalls if late), as a share of the nominal 1x pace (75 s per sim day):
- T=1: 46%.
- T=2: 53%.
- T=2 plus a hedged duplicate at 1 s: 69%, for +18.9% calls.
- T=6 plus a hedge at 1.5 s: 88%.
- 4x is at best 36%.
Hedging assumes the retry's latency is independent of the first call's, which is optimistic.
fundamentals.proposal:
1. Add `THINK_TICKS` (for example 2 ticks, 10 game minutes) to the engine contract. An answer is applied exactly at issueTick+THINK. If it has not arrived, the clock stalls: a barrier in Session.tick() that refuses to step while an overdue request is pending.
2. Hedge any request older than about 1-1.5 s with an idempotent duplicate. The first answer wins and is recorded once.
3. Add a live concurrency semaphore (the lab already uses 24).
4. Jitter scheduled mass decisions (wake-up, reflection) with the seeded RNG across 0-3 ticks.
5. The UI shows the achieved speed; the speed control becomes "max speed".

Live, lab and replay then produce the same world for the same answers at any speed.
fundamentals.unlocks: Authentic decisions that can be compared across runs and experiments, and a stateful world whose history does not depend on which tab or network drove it

fundamentals.title: Take the decision trace out of World; checkpoint only the lean state
fundamentals.problem: `agent.decisions` holds 24 full DecisionRecords per villager: the whole option list, and until 2db20e2 the full state text. It dominates everything that copies or saves the world: checkpoints every 8 s, spectator downloads, ReplayCursor keyframes, structuredClone.
fundamentals.evidence:
world-anatomy.ts, day 7, 15 agents:
- World 2,161 KB, of which decisions are 2,030 KB (94%).
- Lean world 131 KB raw / 19 KB gz; without the static map 92 KB / 15 KB.

lean-checkpoint.ts (latest decision full, history as {tick, picked, p}, map and persona by id, metrics as rounded columns): 250 KB raw / 41 KB gz, 4.5x smaller.

fundamentals.proposal:
Change the Agent type: `decisions` becomes `lastDecision: DecisionRecord | null` plus `history: {tick, kind, picked, pickedLabel, p}[]` (cap 24).
- Full records, including the state text, go to an append-only trace written next to the checkpoint as a delta. For example live/<id>/trace/<day>.jsonl.gz, or IndexedDB for the local role. The inspector's JEV tab lazy-loads from it.
- makeCheckpoint omits tiles, buildings, landmarks, POIs and fields (rebuilt by buildTownMap in hydrateWorld) and personas, which are resolved by id.
- Metrics are stored as a columnar {ticks[], id: number[]} with 3-decimal rounding.
- ReplayCursor keyframes clone the lean world.
fundamentals.unlocks: Cheap, frequent saves for a fully stateful world; spectators and history viewers that scale to 100 villagers and 30+ days

fundamentals.title: Persist the event log as the history: checkpoint plus event tail, pinned to an engine version, streamed to spectators
fundamentals.problem: Checkpoints are the source of truth (good), but the replayable history is not persisted. Session.events lives only in the driving tab's memory: the Checkpoint type in checkpoint.ts has no events field, and after a reload RunRecord.start begins at the resumed world. Genesis replay cannot survive deploys, and every push to main deploys. Spectators adopt a whole new Session from each checkpoint (use-sandbox.ts:330-339), so they see the town jump about 31 ticks every 8 s with no motion.
fundamentals.evidence:
replay-real.ts, the two real Fernhollow records replayed on today's engine: 88 of 387 and 48 of 334 answer events desync.

Within one engine version, replay is fast: 1 day 57-86 ms, 7 days 319-382 ms, 30 days 0.84-1.33 s, 0 desyncs.

In-tab log growth: 1,245 events / 1.4 MB at 7 days, 3,966 events / 4.5 MB at 30 days, lost on reload.

Real records are about 800 B per answer event and 41-45 KB gz per sim day.

wire-size.ts at 1x: the event stream is 923 B per tick (3.5 KB/s). A per-tick view state would be 2.45 KB raw / 468 B gz. Spectators currently pull a 183 KB gz checkpoint every 8 s (about 23 KB/s).
fundamentals.proposal:
- Add `engine: ENGINE_VERSION` (a constant, bumped on any change to engine behaviour) and `eventSeq` to the Checkpoint.
- The driver appends RunEvents in batches with each save, to live/<id>/events/<engineVersion>/<day>.jsonl.gz.
- Resume loads the checkpoint, then applies tail events with eventSeq greater than the checkpoint's, only if the engine version matches.
- The runs viewer replays each segment from its own checkpoint under its own version.
- Spectators long-poll or SSE the event tail and run the same pure engine locally, so they see live motion, falling back to the checkpoint on a version or eventSeq gap.
- Also match answers by (tick, agentId, kind) as a secondary key, so a desync is detected and reported per event.
fundamentals.unlocks: A fully stateful world with a complete, replayable history across reloads and deploys; live-looking spectators; the base for a server-side driver later

fundamentals.title: Honour "stop when I'm not watching" and remove the hidden hard stop (the $10 key budget)
fundamentals.problem: A backgrounded tab is still "open": the worker clock keeps ticking (use-sandbox.ts:92-106, 270-297) and keeps spending with no per-session ceiling, since 2db20e2 removed the 600-call cap. Meanwhile the gateway key's $10 monthly budget (AGENTS.md) acts as an invisible hard cap. When it is exhausted, every /api/jev call fails, and villagers stand still, retrying. Claudio said a closed browser may pause the world, not that a hidden tab should run it for days.
fundamentals.evidence:
From the real runs:
- A 15-villager Fernhollow sim day is 334-387 calls, $0.033-0.037.
- At 1x a sim day is 288 x 260 ms = 75 s. That is about $1.4-1.8 per wall-clock hour (the low end allows for about 16% fewer calls under live latency, per latency-sim.ts), or about $40 a day if a tab is forgotten.
- The $10 monthly key lasts about 6 hours at 1x.
- At 100 villagers, calls per day scale about 7x (fake: 230 to 1,628), about $10-12 an hour at 1x.
fundamentals.proposal:
- Pause the clock when no tab showing the world has been visible for more than about 5 minutes. The driver tracks document.visibilityState, and spectators send a visible-heartbeat through the claim route. Resume on the first visible tab.
- Show a spend meter in the header: this hour, today and this month, from a persisted world.stats.costUsd plus a daily ledger in the checkpoint. This informs; it does not cap.
- Raise or replace the $10 key budget so the world does not silently freeze. If the budget stays, surface a clear "JEV budget exhausted" state instead of a string of per-villager errors.
fundamentals.unlocks: Uncapped JEV exactly as Claudio asked, without a forgotten tab burning money or the world freezing without explanation

fundamentals.title: Population as world state, not config: deterministic births and immigrants with a seeded id and persona generator
fundamentals.problem: createWorld always maps the fixed PERSONAS list (engine.ts:143-192), and WorldConfig holds only seed, scenario and driftModel. A record or config cannot express who exists, so any change in population (reproduction, immigration, more actors) breaks replay. homeOf() scans every building's residents on each call (engine.ts:303-307), and many hot paths call it.
fundamentals.evidence: bench.ts with 30, 60 and 100 agents (clones added after createWorld), replayed from the record: 512 of 527, 982 of 997 and 1,727 of 1,742 events desync. hydrateWorld falls back to fresh.agents[0] for agent ids it does not know (checkpoint.ts:86).
fundamentals.proposal:
- Add `world.agentSeq` and an engine function `spawn(world, spec)` that builds persona, psyche and home deterministically from the world RNG. Trigger it only from engine events (birth after a JEV partnership decision, a scheduled immigrant) or a recorded Intervention {kind: "arrival"}.
- Keep `world.residence: Record<agentId, buildingId>` as an index.
- Checkpoints already carry agents, and replay stays exact because spawning is part of step().
fundamentals.unlocks: Reproduction, more actors and families, with replay and resume that stay exact

fundamentals.title: Canvas: cache what does not animate; draw only on change
fundamentals.problem: Every animation frame redraws the 21 buildings, 6 bushes and every villager pixel by pixel with fillRect, 60 times a second, even when the world is paused (world-canvas.tsx frame(), from line 249). The cost of the character layer grows linearly with population.
fundamentals.evidence:
canvas-count.ts runs the frame() body against a counting context. Per frame: 8,465 fillRect + 6,938 fillStyle sets (15.4K calls).
- Buildings: 5,239 fillRects (62%).
- Characters: 1,582 for 13 villagers (about 120 each).
- Animated tiles: 764 for 86 tiles.
- Bushes: 737 for 6 bushes.
- Labels: 143.
At 100 villagers outside, characters alone would be about 12K fillRects per frame. (I could not time the browser raster: the preview pane will not run scripts from a local file.)
fundamentals.proposal:
- Paint buildings into the static layer, keyed by (lit set, night bucket), and repaint only when those change.
- Cache bushes per berry count.
- Pre-render character sprites per persona x facing x walkFrame into ImageBitmaps, so each villager is one drawImage call.
- Throttle water and fountain animation to about 8 fps, and skip the frame entirely when paused with no camera change.

From the measured layer counts this is under 1K fillRects per frame.
fundamentals.unlocks: 100+ villagers on screen and a quiet CPU when the tab is merely open

fundamentals.title: Index and archive the ever-growing ledgers
fundamentals.problem:
world.crimes, cases, debts, lies and graves, and agent.knows, grow without bound and are scanned linearly in hot paths:
- perceive() walks every debt ever made (engine.ts:977-985).
- settleDebts() does the same every tick.
- The officer's options do knows x crimes.find, plus caseFor = cases.find (engine.ts:1371-1390, 1546).
- exposeLies scans all lies.
CPU is flat today, but snapshot size and O(K·C) scans grow with villagers times days.
fundamentals.evidence: bench 30 days, 15 agents (non-lethal fake): crimes 107, knows 340, debts 56, cases 13, graves 8. Bounded today: memory 14, decisions 24, log 250, drift 60, formative 6. buildOptions stays at 0.11-0.2 ms, so the risk is at 100 villagers x 100 days, not today.
fundamentals.proposal:
- Store crimes and cases as Record<id, ...>, with byCulprit and byCrime indexes.
- Keep per-agent open-debt id lists.
- Make knows a Record<crimeId, tick>.
- Settled debts, closed cases and lies older than LIE_MEMORY_TICKS move out of World into the event log, as they are already recorded there.
fundamentals.unlocks: Long-running worlds (weeks) with justice and economy history that stay cheap to perceive and save
